#9969. Planning with open variable lists in Gecode

A robot needs to fetch a packet from the shelf and put it down on the workbench. Easy enough: drive over to the shelf, pick up the packet, drive back, and put it down. Four actions. Unless the battery is low. Then the robot has to visit the charger first, and the questions become where in the plan that visit should go, and how long the robot should stay there.

This is planning in miniature: a start, some actions, a goal, and nobody telling us how long the plan should be.

Planning is a research field of its own, and a common first idea is to describe the problem in PDDL and hand it to one of the many planning systems that read it. For a lot of problems, that is the right choice. Constraint programming is another natural fit, especially when the actions come with restrictions like a battery that runs down. The common objection is that most constraint programming solvers fix the set of variables before search starts, so we need a bound on the length of the plan before we know how long it will be.

Gecode has always allowed new variables and constraints to be added during search, but before Gecode 6.5.0 there was no explicit support for it. Gecode 6.5.0 adds that support as open variable lists. An OpenIntVarList is a list of ordinary IntVars that are created when propagation or search needs another position, together with an ordinary IntVar for its length. When a position is added, a transition callback can create more variables and post constraints for that step, such as the next state of a plan, so any constraint in Gecode can be used in a model that grows.

In addition, the release has open versions of some common constraints, such as regular, distinct, and sequence, which are posted once on the whole list and follow it as it grows. A list brancher decides both the next value and whether the list should grow, and most of the usual variable and value selectors work on the positions.1 All of this is built with the propagator and brancher interfaces that Gecode already had, plus a few small additions to the kernel.2

The release also includes two experimental search engines, A* and complete anytime beam search. This post models the robot, then the fifteen-puzzle, and ends with the new engines.

The shelf, the workbench, and the charger are connected in a line, in that order, as in the picture at the top. The robot starts at the workbench with one unit of charge. Each move uses one unit, each charge action at the charger adds one, and the battery holds five. Picking up and putting down the packet are free.

With one unit, the robot can reach the shelf, but then it is stuck there with the packet. The shortest working plan visits the charger first.

Three charges are exactly enough, and with two the robot is stuck at the shelf. Charging four or five times also works, but every extra charge makes the plan longer, so the first plan a solver finds need not be the shortest. Try it below, and head straight for the shelf first to see what happens.

Optimal plan: Right → Charge → Charge → Charge → Left → Left → Take packet → Right → Deposit packet

Enable JavaScript to control the robot or play the plan.

What I want is a model that just describes the actions and their effects, and lets the solver discover the detour on its own.

A straightforward CP model has a variable for each action, variables for the state before and after each action, and a transition constraint relating them. For a plan with four actions, there are four action variables and five states, with the first state fixed to the initial situation and the last required to satisfy the goal. For our example, that model has no solution. Planning encodings have traditionally dealt with the unknown length in two ways. One is to solve again with five actions, then six, and so on up to nine, so that the first plan found is also a shortest one. The other is to choose an upper bound, say twelve actions, and allow an unused suffix, at the price of modelling which positions are active and having every position up to the bound in the model from the start.

An open list gives a third option: keep the bound of twelve, but create positions only when search or propagation needs them. The model then grows the way a plan does when you work it out by hand: first the charging visit, then the trip to the shelf, and once the packet is delivered, we can stop.

The full model is in open-robot.cpp. The actions are kept in an open list, and the states between them in three more: where the robot is, how much charge it has, and where the packet is.

Each action is an IntVar over the six action codes, and there are at most twelve of them. actions.length() is the length of the finished plan, and actions.known_length() counts the positions created so far. Creating a position is called materialization, and it does not assign a value.

When the plan grows, the new action is materialized and the callback calls step, which materializes the state after it and posts the constraints between them.

The callback is shared between copies of the space, so it casts the space it is given instead of capturing this. It must also be deterministic, since recomputation and parallel search may repeat an extension in another space.

The legal steps are a table with one tuple for each action and the states before and after it, posted as an extensional constraint for each step.

The plan can only end where the packet has been delivered, and it ends as soon as it has.

Propagation does some planning before search starts. The packet cannot be delivered in fewer than four actions, so the root already has four, the first a move to the shelf or the charger and the second picking up or charging. Branch-and-bound then finds the nine-action plan.

We can also use the regular constraint to encode the state as a transition system, folding the values of at, charge, and packet into the states of a finite automaton instead of keeping them in variables. Each tuple in the table becomes a transition labelled with its action, so the accepted words are exactly the delivery plans.

The model is then just the action list and one constraint, with no state lists and no callback.

The interesting part is what an open regular constraint does with an unfinished plan. After moving to the charger and charging once, the packet is still on the shelf, but the plan can still reach the goal. Moving straight to the shelf is a dead end, and is rejected while the list is still open. So while the list is open, a prefix is kept if it can reach an accepting state within the maximum length, and once it is closed, its last state must be accepting.

Regular propagation works on a layered graph, with a layer of automaton states for each position and edges labelled with the values in each domain. The widget uses a small automaton for the words that start with a and end with b. With a fixed length of two, only ab has a path. The open list has the same two positions but a length of up to four, so a prefix like aa can still become aab. Lower the maximum length to two, and the open list behaves like the fixed one.

Open, so a prefix ending in q₁ can still finish with b.

Gecode does not build the future layers. It computes the shortest distance from each automaton state to an accepting state, and keeps an end state of the prefix only if that distance fits within length().max() - known_length().

Both the table and the automaton list every combination of location, charge, and packet status. That works for the robot, but with more packets and a second robot the combined states explode, and the transitions are better posted as ordinary constraints over the state variables, as in the fifteen-puzzle below.

The list brancher assigns the materialized positions, and once they all have values, it tries closing the list, with extending it as the alternative. For the robot, closing fails until the packet is delivered.

The usual selectors choose among the materialized positions. To settle the number of actions first, branch on the length before the actions, and depth-first search with minimum-value selection then tries shorter plans first.

Building the plan incrementally can find a longer plan before a shorter one, so the companion minimizes the length with branch-and-bound. With -branching max, it tries the highest action code first, which means charging whenever it can, and finds plans of eleven, ten, and finally nine actions.

Real planning models collect side rules: don’t repeat an action, don’t keep the charger busy too long, pick up before you deliver. The open constraints in the release express rules like these, posted once and applied to every new position.

The last three assume other open lists, of jobs, loads, and battery levels. Side rules can change which plans exist at all. For the robot, forbidding immediate repeats leaves no plan, since a single charge never pays for the trip there and back, while at most three charges in every window of four removes the two longer plans and keeps the nine-action one.

What makes these constraints different from their closed versions is the positions that do not exist yet. sequence and sliding_sum only count complete windows, so a plan shorter than the window is unrestricted. distinct remembers the assigned values and removes them from positions created later. min and max can only bound the result from one side while the list is open, since a later position can still lower the minimum or raise the maximum.

The fifteen-puzzle is the classic test problem for heuristic search, with far too many boards for a table or an automaton. Fifteen numbered tiles and a blank occupy a four-by-four board, and a move slides a tile next to the blank into the blank. The goal has the tiles in order, with the blank at the bottom right. This board needs two moves: slide tile 14 left, and then tile 15.

Click a tile beside the blank to slide it. With the board focused, arrow keys move the blank.

Seen from the blank, it moves right twice, so a plan can be described by the successive positions of the blank. Gecode’s fifteen-puzzle.cpp uses two open lists: path[i] is the cell of the blank in board i, and the sixteen entries from tiles[16*i] are board i, with 0 for the blank.

Only path has a transition callback, which creates the board for each new blank position.

The constructor body ties the two lengths together, fixes the first board, and bounds the length from below.

The Manhattan distance, the sum of each tile’s distance to its goal cell, is a lower bound on the number of moves, so propagation creates several boards before any move is chosen. Each new blank position materializes its board, connects it to the previous one, and posts the goal, just like the robot’s step.

A slide moves the blank to a neighbouring cell, puts the moved tile in the old blank cell, and leaves every other cell unchanged.

Every board is a permutation of the tiles, so an assigned path determines all the boards, and it is enough to branch on path.

The example also has a fixed model, -model fixed, that creates every board up to the move limit and uses a branch filter so that search does not choose moves after the goal. For a two-move solution with a limit of eight, it has nine boards where the open model has three.

This finds plans of eight, six, and finally four moves, which matches the initial Manhattan distance, and -model fixed finds the same optimum.

Gecode 6.5.0 also includes two experimental search engines, AStar and CABS (complete anytime beam search), enabled with GECODE_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL=ON in CMake or --enable-experimental with Autoconf. They work with any Gecode space, with or without open lists, and their APIs may still change.

Branch-and-bound explores depth-first, and has no idea which of the pending partial plans looks most promising. Heuristic search estimates how good the best completion of each partial plan can be, and explores the most promising ones first. It is also the workhorse behind many of the planning systems mentioned at the start. The estimate must be admissible, never above the true cost. For the robot, ignoring the battery gives one: after moving to the charger and charging once, two actions are used and at least five remain, a bound of seven where the true total is nine.

Both engines take a Search::HeuristicGuidance, whose bound callback returns an optimistic value for the total objective, including the cost so far, and must be exact on solutions. For the puzzle, the bound is the number of moves made so far plus the Manhattan distance of the board they lead to.

depth stops at the first undecided move, even when later boards have been created, and the length gives the bound instead when it is stronger.

Both engines use the model’s constrain to require improvement after each solution, so as with branch-and-bound, the first solution need not be optimal. A* keeps every pending state. CABS keeps only a beam of candidates at each layer of the search tree, starting with a width of one and doubling it while the discarded candidates might still lead to a better solution. That finds a plan quickly, and spends more effort later on improving it and proving optimality. CABS can also use a dominance test, which discards a candidate when another one can match each of its completions with one that is no worse.

Gecode’s tsptw.cpp, for the travelling salesman problem with time windows, offers all three engines on a closed model. I wrote an open-list variant that creates each position of the tour when the tour reaches it. Every tour visits all customers, so stating its length would create every position at the root. Instead, the variant states the goal as a condition on the visited customers.

Both models find and prove the optimal travel times for the two built-in instances with branch-and-bound, A*, and CABS. The instances are far too small to say which combination works best on hard problems.

Leaving future positions uncreated is a tradeoff. They take no storage, but their domains are not available for propagation either, so a fixed-horizon model may detect some failures earlier. My guess is that open lists pay off when a large upper bound is needed to admit all plans, while most of the search works with much shorter prefixes, but that needs measuring. For classical planning problems, a dedicated planner will often be the better tool. A constraint model becomes interesting when the plan also has to satisfy side constraints, like resource limits, time windows, or the rules above.

Back in the workshop, the model is the same whatever the initial charge. With a full battery, the shortest plan is the direct four actions, and with a single unit, it is the nine-action detour. Nobody had to guess the length of the plan in advance. The model describes what the robot can do, and search works out how long it takes.

The exceptions are the activity-based (Action) and conflict-history (CHB) variable selectors. They require the complete list to be materialized when the brancher is posted, so they cannot be used for positions created later. ↩

For example, callbacks run inside a Space::NoGPI scope, so that propagators created and discarded during search do not accumulate global propagator information such as the accumulated failure count (AFC). A callback can open a Space::UseGPI scope for postings that should be tracked as usual. ↩

InfoQ Homepage News Spring News Roundup: First Release Candidates of Boot, Framework, Data, Security, Modulith, AI

Oct 31, 2026 6 min read

There was a flurry of activity during the week of October 19th, 2026, highlighting: first release candidates of: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Data, Spring Cloud, Spring Security, Spring for GraphQL, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOS, Spring Modulith, Spring REST Docs, Spring AI, Spring Batch, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka, Spring LDAP and Spring Web Services.

The first release candidate of Spring Boot 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a migration to the Ubuntu Resolute builder replacing the Noble Java Tiny Builder; and improved Uber-Jar performance using direct lookup of classes and resources in nested jars. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

The first release candidate of Spring Framework 7.1.0 ships with bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: improved nullability in the DataAccessUtils and LinkedCaseInsensitiveMap classes; and new overloaded methods, onRetrySuccess() and onRetryFailure(), defined in the RetryListener interface, that add an instance of the RetryState class in the parameter list such that listeners can access the retry state directly upon failure. Further details on this release, including removal of deprecated APIs, may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Data 2026.1.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades, RC1 upgrades to all of the subprojects and a notable new feature in Spring Data Redis that now forwards subscription notifications related to annotated listener methods if a bean implements the SubscriptionListener interface.

The first release candidate of Spring Cloud 2026.0.0, codenamed Paddington, delivers dependency upgrades, RC1 upgrades to all of the subprojects and a notable change where Spring Cloud Bus is no longer its own project and has been incorporated into Spring Cloud Stream. This release is based on Spring Boot 4.2.0-RC1. More details on this release may be found in this release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Security 7.2.0 ships with bug fixes, dependency upgrades and two new features: an instance of the StrictServerWebExchangeFirewall class no longer detects a non-canonical-case HTTP method as a distinct value due to a change in the valueOf() method, defined in the Spring Framework HttpMethod class, that now normalizes casing; and RestClientOpaqueTokenIntrospector and SpringOpaqueTokenIntrospector classes now set the Content-Type header to application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and this what's new page.

The first release candidate of Spring for GraphQL 2.1.0 provides one bug fix that reinstates the Content-Length response header for WebFlux applications so that backwards compatibility is maintained and notable dependency upgrades such as: Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1; Spring Data 2026.1.0-RC1; and Spring Security 7.2.0-RC1. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Session 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: integrating the Spring Security Settings Plugin and Spring Security Maven Plugin; and standardizing the configuration of the public and private continuous integration environments. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Integration 7.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a deprecation of the default constructor in the SerializingHttpMessageConverter class to define a new constructor that contains the allowedPatterns attribute for improved security; and the ability to allow the DefaultJmsHeaderMapper class to set the outboundHeaderNames, inboundHeaderNames and excludedOutboundStandardRequestHeaderNames and excludedInboundStandardResponseHeaderNames to align with the DefaultHttpHeaderMapper class. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring HATEOAS 3.2.0 provides notable dependency upgrades such as: Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1; Spring Plugin 4.2.0-RC1; and Reactor 2026.0.0-RC1. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Modulith 2.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new ABANDONED and RESUBMITTED enumerations, added to the EventPublication.Status interface, to distinguish between failed and abandoned event publications; and event publications are now completed, by default, using the Spring Framework TransactionSynchronization interface within a listener's transaction to avoid the possibility of a listener committing and the completion to fail. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring REST Docs 4.1.0 ships with one bug fix, a dependency upgrade to Spring Framework 7.1.0-RC1 and new features such as: improved nullability using JSpecify; and support for using the Spring Framework RestTestClient interface. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring AI 2.1.0 provides dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new SessionService interface for creating and finding sessions that replaces the now-deprecated ChatMemory interface; and the ability for the OpenAiChatModel and DeepSeekChatModel classes to build an assistant message of each choice from ordered message parts. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring Batch 6.1.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new @JobParameter annotation that injects a job parameter into a job or step scoped bean used to require a Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expression; and a new PageableItemReader class that serves as a type-safe alternative to RepositoryItemReader class to take a function from the Spring Data Pageable interface to a Slice interface. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring AMQP 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: removal of the use of the noNullElements() method, defined in the Spring Framework Assert class, to allow the RabbitAdmin class and AmqpAdmin interface to accept null or empty arrays when declaring exchanges, queues, and bindings; and a simplification of the buildMessage() method, defined in both the AbstractAdaptableMessageListener and MessagingMessageListenerAdapter classes, to avoid unnecessary nesting when handling existing instances of the Message class and message conversion. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring for Apache Kafka 4.2.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and one new feature that now writes out the value defined in the KafkaHeaders.DELIVERY_ATTEMPT header when using the CommonDelegatingErrorHandler class in conjunction with the deliveryAttemptHeader container property set to true. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.

The first release candidate of Spring LDAP 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: use of string parameterization in logging to avoid non-constant filename lengths; the addition of test cases for the DefaultObjectDirectoryMapperTests class; and string cleanup in the getStringAttribute() method, defined in DirContextAdapter class, to prevent a ClassCastException. More details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes and what's new page.

The first release candidate of Spring Web Services 5.1.0 ships with documentation improvements dependency upgrades and one new feature that allows an instance of the DefaultWsdl11Definition class to attach a policy document, such as a WS-Policy or WS-SecurityPolicy fragment, to every binding it generates. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

#9967. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

The same snippet runs unchanged on NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (ROCm) and Intel (XPU) GPUs, device_map="auto" places the model on whichever accelerator is available.

After loading the model, you can do text-only inference with it as follows.

We would need torchvision to be able to use images and text.

Muse Glimmer accepts images as input, as demonstrated here:

To work with videos we recommend installing torchcodec into the environment.

Muse Glimmer can answer complex questions about videos without audio. You can do video inference as follows, here’s an example from VideoMME2, which is the most popular video question answering benchmark.

Muse Glimmer can do multimodal tool calling, here’s how you can do it. In the example below, we ask the model to call the weather tool based on the city in the image.

You can use Muse Glimmer to do open ended object detection in images as follows.

Here is an end to end script to perform object detection GitHub Gist

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 llama.cpp support. Meta has distributed calibrated quants in this repo, and Unsloth is releasing optimized quants as well. DFlash speculative decoding is supported as well. You can use a pre-built llama binary to start a llama server or a CLI. To install llama.cpp, run:

Then you can start the server as follows.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:8080 to chat with the built-in WebUI.

You can also query the server as follows.

You can also use llama server with coding agents like Pi.

DFlash uses a lightweight block-diffusion drafter model to provide same output with extra speed-ups in decoding phase. Transformers and llama.cpp ship support for DFlash drafter of Muse Glimmer day-0.

Below you can see how speculative decoding can speed-up generation in realistic setups. The video shows llama.cpp webui with DFlash on the left and regular generation on the right.

You can load the drafter and model as follows, and infer like how you would with base model with an additional parameter (shown in the upcoming snippets).

You can start llama server using following command. --spec-draft-n-max argument controls how many future tokens DFlash proposes during each speculative-decoding step. Muse Glimmer’s DFlash model was trained with a block size of 16, one anchor token plus 15 proposed tokens, so any value above 15 will be clamped to 15.

You can also use llama cli with speculative decoding drafter as follows.

For a managed, autoscaling deployment, open the Muse Glimmer 30B Inference Endpoints preset. The model is already selected: choose the organization, cloud provider, region, compatible GPU instance, authentication, and autoscaling settings, then review the hourly price and click Create Endpoint. Once its status is Running, you can test it in the Playground and copy the endpoint URL and model name from the Overview.

The deployed model exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. Keep your Hugging Face token in an environment variable, set HF_ENDPOINT_URL to the URL shown in the Overview without /v1, and set HF_ENDPOINT_MODEL to the endpoint's model name.

See the Inference Endpoints documentation for configuration, autoscaling, security, logs, and monitoring.

For this release, we ship support for vLLM with transformers backend.

You can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

As part of this release, we ship an example to fine-tune Muse Glimmer on small split of MolmoWeb dataset. This shows how to make model generate structured outputs and how to fine-tune on images.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

Set HF_TOKEN in the OpenClaw gateway environment, then add this to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Use the exact model ID returned by the endpoint’s /v1/models response if it differs.

If we hook up Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face MCP and update its AGENTS.md we give it the capability to find a quantized version of itself on the hub and run locally. This is handy if you want to work on something private, or just cut costs.

If you do this a second time, Muse Glimmer will find the cached weights and switch to them, so feel free to add a convenient command like /spawn.

Finally, let’s get Muse Glimmer to do some light RSI. We can instruct our agent to optimize its own inference engine for specific hardware, in this case a Nvidia H100. To do this, the agent will need to use another inference engine, like Inference Endpoints above.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#9965. My favourite laptop

I’m not a big owner of things, but the best laptop I’ve ever owned is a roughed-up 2015 Thinkpad X250.

For the flex, here it is running a GUI shell sat on top of the microkernel I’m currently working on (blog post about this incoming… eventually).

Here’s a list of things that I think make it brilliant. I don’t want to pretend that any of these things are uniquely exemplary: far from it. It is the confluence of them, and not any one in particular, that makes me love using it.

It’s pretty tiny. Its form-factor fits snuggly into the footprint of an A4 piece of paper, so it sits alongside books and folders when placed in a small rucksack without risking damage.

It weighs almost nothing too: even with the extra capacity battery, it’s only about 1.45 Kg. Light enough that you almost don’t notice it when travelling.

Mine has an i5-5200U: 4 logical cores, maxing out at 2.7 GHz. I upgraded it to 8 GB of RAM a while back: more than enough for some light on-the-go programming.

Even at full pelt, I’ve never heard the fan kicking up much of a fuss. Now that I think about it, I’m not even certain that it works.

The X250 has both an internal battery and an external battery slot. I’ve opted for the largest after-market external battery I could find. When doing casual work the laptop will easily survive for north of 10 hours without a charge, stretching to 12 hours if I’m careful.

The X250 was quite popular and replacement parts retail very cheaply on ebay. It’s not the easiest to disassemble Thinkpad by any means but I can tear it apart entirely with the pocket phillips I keep on my keyring. I have previously replaced:

Every time you open up a laptop you run the risk of damaging something important either via a slip of the hand or simply the accumulated toll of loosening and tightening dozens of tiny screw threads. Despite that, my X250 has proved remarkably resilient and has never sustained any major damage despite more than more than a dozen tear-downs.

As with most Thinkpads, the keyboard feels lovely to use. When you spend a lot of time writing code the reliability and sensitivity of a keyboard starts to matter a lot. Coupled with my text editor, the experience of writing code on the thing is beautifully snappy.

I opted for Endeavour OS. In the usual Arch Linux tradition, it favours native package installs over sandboxed applications. As a result my install sits at around 30 GB. A 128 GB M.2 SSD raided from another second-hand machine is more than enough to cover that and everything I’m working on.

I’ve slimmed down my systemd setup as much as possible and the thing boots from cold in about 8 seconds.

Here’s where the X250 beats out most competition. I bought mine second-hand for about £100 in 2018. They’ve only got cheaper since then. I’m not afraid to take it anywhere because it’s barely worth stealing and would be cheap to replace even if that were to happen. Its value is very much not in its on-paper specs and instead in how I use it.

I get a certain glee in keeping older or second-hand hardware running as a daily driver. It sounds silly, but it feels like a quiet revolt against bigger-faster-costlier consumption culture. Come the end times, this is the machine I’ll be riding it out with.

#9963. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

InfoQ Homepage News OpenBSD 8.0 Brings Expanded Hardware Support, Security Enhancements, and Virtualization Improvements

Oct 31, 2026 2 min read

OpenBSD 8.0 is a substantial upgrade bringing broader hardware compatibility, enhanced security, an expanded virtual address space, and support for modern architectures, including Intel Arc A-Series graphics support, ARM64 hibernation, RISC-V improvements, and enhanced virtual machine support.

Key hardware and virtualization improvements in OpenBSD 8.0 include a larger virtual address space for the AMD64 kernel, expanded from 4 GB to 512 GB, enabling it to map graphics cards with more than 4 GB of VRAM; support for multi-processor virtual machines through vmm/vmd, with up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest and improvements to virtual hardware and guest compatibility; expanded RISC-V support, including the 'V' vector extension and Advanced Interrupt Architecture, improving compatibility with newer processors and platforms; and arm64 hibernation support, alongside faster swap encryption using AES instructions.

Although OpenBSD 8.0 introduces support for the Intel Arc A-Series GPUs, based on the DG2/Alchemist architecture, NVIDIA GPUs remain unsupported, partially due to the fact that NVIDIA does not provide proprietary binary drivers for OpenBSD, unlike Linux and FreeBSD.

OpenBSD 8.0 also expands peripheral support, including the riscv64 K3 PCIe/USB3 combo PHY, the SpacemiT K3 SoC and PCIe controller, as well as the Intel E610 and Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake Ethernet devices. New drivers are now available for Samsung Advanced BIOS Interface (SABI), Rockchip OTP memory, and Samsung laptop battery monitor. Wireless adapters support has been significantly expanded as well, including support for the Qualcomm Technologies WCN7850 wireless network in the qwz driver.

The httpd daemon in OpenBSD 8.0 has received several enhancements, including support for custom HTTP headers, header block/drop rules for request filtering, improved default crypto methods for HTTPS, and cache control for static files.

On the security front, OpenBSD 8.0 continues to emphasize security as a defining priority with an outstanding track record:

We remain proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install.

The new release incorporates LibreSSL 4.4.0, which introduces numerous compatibility-layer fixes for AIX, FreeBSD, macOS, MinGW, NetBSD, and especially Windows, alongside various internal improvements. It also brings OpenSSH 10.6, which disables SSH Compression using LZ77 and rejects $ and \ characters in command-line usernames to mitigate potential shell injection vulnerabilities, among other enhancements.

A Hacker News thread about the new release highlighted several important aspects of OpenBSD. User ctolsen emphasized the system's simplicity and its adherence to traditional Unix philosophy:

OpenBSD just feels like a *nix system is supposed to. ps aux is like 10 entries at first. pf makes so much sense. man pages are consistently incredible. The security/cryptography focus, managing services, pledge/unveil...

Longtime OpenBSD user nanolith, who has used the system for nearly 20 years, praised its stability and consistency across upgrades, noting that "it's so stable that I barely notice changes when I upgrade until I go hunting for them". However, he also points out that OpenBSD might not be the best choice for large servers, given its lack of support for advanced filesystems like ZFS, Btrfs, or GeFS.

#9961. How We Could Have Backdoored Bash (Hacktron blog)

Given the increase in supply chain attacks, I really don't understand why so many projects still feel comfortable to fully rely on centralized, server-side security mechanisms. Almost every time I look at a real or potential supply chain attack, I cannot help but wonder how much more difficult or fragile the attack would have been if regular code signing would be more ubiquitous.

Almost every modern system has a HSM, Secure Enclave, or whatever; and if you don't like those, there are OpenPGP-smartcards, YubiKeys, ... you name it. If you don't like PGP, OpenSSH also supports signing for over six years now, including FIDO2-backed signatures. Git support for OpenPGP signatures goes back for decades, and OpenSSH signatures are also supported for more than 5 years now. Yet, nobody seems to care – worse, even basic infrastructure like cargo, pip, npm, etc., don't offer an optional possibility to attach and require signatures.

To be clear: I neither blame individual developers nor maintainers; I'm a big fan of provided-as-is – nobody should be forced to buy a YubiKey just because they are hobby devs. Nonetheless if we operate at an institutional scale, where we have legal entities and supply core infrastructure... I don't get it – not even to blame someone, I just simply don't get it.

Classical banking provides a more nuanced (if less formalized) picture. Entities have credit risk, collateral must be made available, and all sorts of derivatives are traded against those things. The trading is both hedging (to protect yourself against a business partner's default) and speculative (because you have an opinion about their decline or recovery). Clearing houses like the Options Clearing Corporation create a safe harbor for mutual trust by holding its members to a high standard of credit-worthiness. In technology we have lots of perfectly correct, cryptographically-sound signing solutions. We don't have the semi-formal credit systems that banking has shown to mostly work. I think this is largely because trust is radically efficient, and mistrust carries a lot of overhead and capital drag. It's better if we can rely on trust, but best if we could formalize credit efficiently and solve for distributed trust management.

In technology we have lots of perfectly correct, cryptographically-sound signing solutions. We don't have the semi-formal credit systems that banking has shown to mostly work. I think this is largely because trust is radically efficient, and mistrust carries a lot of overhead and capital drag. It's better if we can rely on trust, but best if we could formalize credit efficiently and solve for distributed trust management.

Even if you have full cryptographic signing, there are still classes of attacks that compromise the keys or certificates and break it open.

Definitely, trust is hard, and code signing is by no means a silver bullet; it only helps against certain attack scenarios, and also has to be applied correctly. Nonetheless, E2E signature chains make a lot of attacks much harder or fragile or – in abstract terms – more expensive.

It's a bit like saying: TLS is not perfect, CAs are not secure, and someone might roll a private key of 4 (obligatory xkcd). Nonetheless, nobody would seriously argue that we probably should ditch TLS and go back to plain HTTP.

Of course, this doesn't scale well (especially to regular people which often don't even know what TLS is), but if you don't need to trust many web servers (and I don't) and your users are capable of verifying a PGP signature manually (mine can), it can be enough.

I might be wrong there, but I had the impression that if the user chooses to import your site's certificate system-wide the only option they have for that is to make it a trust anchor, and therefore allow it to act as a CA, because (from my understanding) quite a few TLS clients assume that all trust anchors are inherently allowed to act as CAs, and cert extensions like basicConstraints (which says "this is an end entity and not a CA") are only honored at least one level down from that. So if I've got that right, then making your users treat each web or TLS server as a potential CA exposes them to more risk (as each server has its key online) compared to having a real personal CA (whose key you can guard properly). This is on top of needing to repeat the PGP verification step manually for each new server (or each new key rotation), rather than verifying the private CA just once... (And of course trust anchors can't be revoked except for everyone removing them manually, whereas if your one server's key is compromised, your private CA can issue a CRL – which most of Linux TLS ecosystem sadly doesn't check, lagging 30 years behind other platforms, but at least I think the major web browsers do.)

So if I've got that right, then making your users treat each web or TLS server as a potential CA exposes them to more risk (as each server has its key online) compared to having a real personal CA (whose key you can guard properly). This is on top of needing to repeat the PGP verification step manually for each new server (or each new key rotation), rather than verifying the private CA just once... (And of course trust anchors can't be revoked except for everyone removing them manually, whereas if your one server's key is compromised, your private CA can issue a CRL – which most of Linux TLS ecosystem sadly doesn't check, lagging 30 years behind other platforms, but at least I think the major web browsers do.)

That's not a big deal. I assume and ask users to assume that my server is not trusted, and that the only things they can trust from it are the PGP-signed commits in the git repositories. The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult.

For v3 certificates CA:FALSE is also the default if the whole extension is absent. The point though is that trust anchors have different treatment from regular certificates. I've heard that some platforms ignore most of the metadata of a cert that's been specified as a trust anchor (e.g. root CA expiry dates certainly seem to be commonly ignored), and/or the fact that they're installed into a "Trusted *authorities*" store is interpreted as a user override of the CA:FALSE, and/or something along those lines. So if one tells users "install my web server's self-signed certificate into /etc/ssl/certs, it has CA:FALSE so it's safe", I'd be more than a little cautious about that. Well, of course, the same goes for a whole personal CA – but what I mean to say is, telling users "install my whole CA into /etc/ssl/certs" is *explicitly* an informed trust decision, while telling users "install my web server cert into /etc/ssl/certs" can be an accidental trust decision that *looks* like it is scoped to a single server but secretly is much broader. Yes, I too would love the ability to install TLS CAs that are scoped to a single domain subtree (like how it is possible with OpenSSH's certificates), or at least wider support of 'nameConstraints' (the extension that truly restricts a CA to only your domain and which half the things happily ignore). But unfortunately we're not even at the point yet where most Linux software could distinguish basic trust purposes - only Mozilla's NSS has distinct "trusted for TLS" and "trusted for S/MIME", and p11-kit has been *trying* to expose that to the broader ecosystem, but most software is still at the caveman level of "everything in ca-certificates.pem is trusted permanently for every purpose"... > I've been considering that option. I'm not experienced enough in OpenSSL to have a CA myself, but I'd consider eventually having one. Of course, I'd like to restrict it to emitting certificates for my domains only, and I'd sign the CA itself with my PGP key, but indeed, it would be an improvement over what I'm doing now. Honestly OpenSSL's own tooling isn't great, it has an "openssl ca" but its usability is, ehh. The "easy-rsa" script that comes with OpenVPN might be an improvement. For a GUI, the Qt-based XCA seemed alright as well. (Smallstep (step-ca) also seems relatively popular but it is Infrastructure, not a standalone tool. It didn't quite click for me; I ended up writing my own CA in Ruby's openssl libraries, then another using python-certbuilder, then another using python-cryptography...) > The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult. I think those are rather intertwined. On the one hand, if all you want is encryption, you don't even need the "PGP verification" part at all, just throw together any dummy certificate and it'll do the job (since encryption is negotiated regardless of any certificate). But on the other hand, authenticating the server (as in the endpoint of the connection, not the data it serves) is what ultimately prevents people from injecting ads or "other stuff" when they really want.

I think those are rather intertwined. On the one hand, if all you want is encryption, you don't even need the "PGP verification" part at all, just throw together any dummy certificate and it'll do the job (since encryption is negotiated regardless of any certificate). But on the other hand, authenticating the server (as in the endpoint of the connection, not the data it serves) is what ultimately prevents people from injecting ads or "other stuff" when they really want.

FWIW, most (all?) GNU projects GPG-sign their release tarballs and release git tags. For GNU coreutils and Gnulib, our repository is mirrored in many places, some automatically syncing from Savannah and some not. So, if this issue were abused, it certainly wouldn't be good, but it wouldn't be unrecoverable. Anyways, it is very refreshing to see a software security company disclose these issues responsibly, and follow it up with an article that is not condescending to the project in discussion and which voices their good intentions: > Like much of the infrastructure free software depends on, it’s run by a handful of volunteers and FSF staff with limited resources. We wanted to put our resources to work there. Many thanks to them for that, and for catching these issues.

This sounds like git commits are not necessarily signed; is there a technical or operational reason for this? Because I imagine that you could use such a backdoor to subtly inject or rewrite commits, and those changes would inadvertently end up inside the signed tarballs as well?

Even with SHA-1, this is not feasible. While the collision resistance of SHA-1 is broken and you can craft special pairs of inputs that share the same arbitrary hash, the pre-image resistance still is comparatively solid – finding a different input for a given hash is still not practical.

There are some attacks for very long messages (2^100 operations for 2^60 bytes), but for the given scenario "commit hashes unchanged [aka given] and the diffs relatively similar", there are no known attacks against SHA-1. We still should probably switch to SHA-2 sooner than later nonetheless; but for this specific requirement, SHA-1 is still more than strong enough for now.

While the collision resistance of SHA-1 is broken and you can craft special pairs of inputs that share the same arbitrary hash, ...

So this just adds one more layer to the attack. Before you change the git repository you need to craft this pair of commits, one with a genuine bug fix that you sneak into the repository and another one additionally containing an evil payload. Once you have access to the repository you can switch out the commits.

Yes, this sounds far fetched, but not so much after the xz utils attack.

We still should probably switch to SHA-2 sooner than later nonetheless;

Well, neither commit it going to look normal. There's going to be 128 binary bytes in there as the algorithm tries to make two files with the same hash. Then they have a common suffix. So the good and evil payload exist in both commits, you just have to find 128 bytes which are somehow going to select the evil or the good payload. In the actual attack it involved a file with a pdf and an embedded jpeg. In pdf there is lots of room to hide stuff, in source code not so much. A chosen prefix attack would be more dangerous but AFAIK does not exist. Besides the fact that GitHub (and other libraries) have code to detect this attack.

If you have A-B-[you merge C]-C'-[others pull]-[others push]-[you pull because others pushed], you will be the only one who has a diverging history. Now, if that is a problem depends on your git config – if you have pull.ff, git will abort; but if you have pull.rebase or pull.no-rebase, you need to be rather vigilant to notice anything.

As an attacker, I probably would also try to insert a new commit instead of rewriting one; but on the other hand if you know that people are using (no-)rebase, a silent rewrite would be really hard to detect afterwards. And (no-)rebase is not super uncommon in my experience, because depending on how you or your team work, feature branches are not necessarily linear.

If I were an attacker, I think crafting an evil Merge remote-branch 'master' into 'my-topic' commit which adds the evil content among a sea of "sync" changes in a contribution would be a juicy target. Especially in squash merge workflows.

I really need to finish the "reject up-merges" check to ban such "wrong way" merges…but any merge commit is ripe for abuse. At least in the standard forge-based flows. Email, Gerrit, and other per-patch mechanisms would be "immune" from it just by the fact that they don't handle merge commit contributions like that.

The default Git setup on Savannah--or at least groff's--is configured to not allow force pushes at all. That's a little frustrating for me, because I'd prefer to have public "feature branches" or, for example right now, a "post-1.25" branch since we're in a (sort of) code freeze for the 1.25.0 release. But for the way I work, there's no point having a feature branch if I can't rewrite its history aggressively, because I make lots of mistakes and change my mind frequently. I think I asked once if force-pushes could be enabled for certain branches, but I don't recall ever getting an answer. But if this policy keeps Savannah safer from a supply-chain attack, I won't grumble.

Not to mention that while people sort of know how to make spot human decentralized release signing work untangling the needs of mostly automated pre-release code pipelines (continuous testing of commits, MRs and dependencies) would require some major investigation and rethinking by someone.

#9960. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.
