#9927. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

InfoQ Homepage Articles Systemic Approach to Memory, Knowledge, and Context in Agentic AI Architectures

Nov 02, 2026 16 min read

As the industry moves from chatbots to autonomous agents, the architectural bottleneck is shifting. The hard problem is no longer simply retrieving data. It is deciding what an agent should know, when it should know it, how long it should remember it, and what should be forgotten. As with humans, it is one thing to know and another to remember. Hence, memory and knowledge. Knowing when to use any of the existing "knows" by bringing it to memory depends on the task context. For example, if I want to cook an omelet, I don’t necessarily need to remember how to knead dough right now.

Automated code transformation at scale. Fix vulnerabilities, migrate frameworks, and modernize legacy code across every repo. Try Moderne Free.

Agents must reason across tools, sessions, users, and live systems, given that in an engineered system we can describe the context as a control plane. Context as a control plane is an architectural paradigm in which organizational, behavioral, and situational data (the who, what, and why) serve as the centralized governing layer for system operations, rather than being hardcoded directly into individual applications, AI models, or microservices. In our world, this will determine whether an agent acts like a reliable software system. Providing the wrong context highly increases the likelihood of the model hallucinating.

Knowledge of the system is our policies, governance, and hard truth. Knowledge acts as the system’s official textbook. It holds core business logic, strict policies, and databases. Back to our omelet example, part of the knowledge would be the need for eggs and a pan.

Memory is the critical layer that bridges historical data and real-time signals into a reasoning-ready state. What needs to be remembered for the current task? This is usually information given from knowledge, historical data, and current live events.

Our goal in agentic systems is, when given the task context, system knowledge, and memory, to turn data into the right memory state at the right moment.

Beyond that, there are limitations to this dynamic architecture paradigm; hence, we need to systematically address the economic costs of large language model (LLM) limitations and the technical, architectural roots of hallucinations. As developers and architects, learning to avoid the common "culprits" of agentic systems mismanagement is crucial. Dive in to learn how to design a sophisticated, multi-tiered architecture for the next generation of reliable agentic AI.

An LLM is only as good as how we use it. While the model generates, our system determines what it sees. To avoid hallucinations, we need a trustworthy system around it. Leveraging context, knowledge, and memory. To architect the system, we will separate the model from the surrounding machinery. Going forward, for the machinery around it, we will call it a context engine. The context engine is part of the context control plane. This is the orchestrator responsible for selecting, filtering, ranking, structuring, compressing, safeguarding, and delivering information before it ever hits the LLM inference endpoint. It pulls information from knowledge, categorizes it in memory, and determines what the agent's context should be at any given millisecond. This is a meaningful shift from simple prompt engineering to systems engineering.

Prompt engineering assumes the task is to craft a better instruction. Context engineering assumes the real task is to build a dynamic substrate that continuously assembles the right state for reasoning. The prompt is no longer about "What should I ask the model?" It is "What is the minimal, highest-value context the model needs in order to reason well right now?"

In a production-grade agentic architecture, we require dynamic systems that dictate what an agent "knows" at any given millisecond. Our system goal is to take what’s relevant and compile a new prompt encompassing the required information to improve the model's success likelihood.

To understand how the Context Engine behaves, consider the analogy of a modern software compiler. A compiler translates high-level source code into machine-executable instructions; the context engine translates vast oceans of unstructured, disconnected raw, real-time, and historical data into a structured, reasoning-ready state. It builds a deterministic state machine that allows the probabilistic agent to execute safely. It ensures that inputs are authenticated, validated against business logic, stripped of personally identifiable information (PII), and securely sandboxed before the LLM generates a plan of action.

Effective software architecture for autonomous AI agents requires reconciling several fundamentally conflicting paradigms of data management and data flow.

A robust agentic architecture must gracefully balance long-term "episodic" memory with immediate "sensory" input. Meaning that to build a useful context engine, our architecture must reconcile two very different categories of state: historical memory and real-time input.

Historical memory is the long-lived layer. It includes prior interactions, past decisions, user preferences, domain rules, internal documentation, and accumulated observations. This is what gives an agent continuity. It allows the system to behave as though it has experience.

Real-time input is the short-lived layer. It includes the current task, the latest events, live telemetry, fresh tool outputs, and environmental changes. This is what keeps the agent grounded in the present.

While vector databases excel at retrieving historical, semantic facts, agentic workflows frequently pivot on sub-second, real-time context. For example, if an AI DevOps agent is triaging a server outage, retrieving an architectural runbook from a vector store (episodic memory) is only half the battle. The agent also needs the live error log stream from the last five seconds (sensory memory). The architecture must fuse these batch and streaming sources asynchronously, ensuring the agent acts on a unified, up-to-date reality.

This architecture must have balance. If it over-indexes on history/episodic memory, the agent becomes stale. It will keep replaying yesterday’s assumptions into today’s reality. If it over-indexes on real-time data, the agent becomes reactive and forgetful. It may respond to the latest signal but fail to incorporate the broader context that gives that signal meaning.

Luckily for us, this tension is not new. Distributed systems have always had to reconcile durable state with transient events. Agent systems inherit the same problem, but with an additional challenge: the reasoning layer is probabilistic, expensive, and bounded by a limited context window. This adds an important layer of constraint optimization to the context architecture design - deciding which information to keep, which can be compressed, which must be revalidated, and which should be excluded entirely. The goal is not just freshness or completeness. The goal is usefulness under constraint.

Figure 1: Historical Data vs Real-Time Memory Streams (Source: created by the author with Gemini)

One of the most common architectural mistakes in AI systems is treating retrieval as if it were enough, ie, operating under the semantic equivalent of a SQL SELECT *, assuming more information must be better. Architectures that attempt to consistently retrieve large volumes of data will inevitably fail at scale. We can think of retrieval as how we get data into the system, yet it does not guarantee that the data is useful, timely, coherent, or appropriately ranked for the decision at hand. This is what standard RAG pipelines are all about. They are often built to retrieve raw, fragmented, and overlapping data chunks. In actuality, using this approach would most likely result in the system dumping 10 unedited wiki pages into a prompt, making the LLM waste compute cycles trying to sort the noise from the signal - yet failing due to relevant signals buried under less important and more noisy ones. Hence, the right information and shape of the data, which we refer to as knowledge, matter more than raw data.

True Knowledge Curation focuses on cumulative insight. Instead of injecting raw data, the architecture employs background workers/ML pipelines that distill, aggregate, and rank retrieved data by relevance, using the up-to-date system state. To achieve that, we need to build dedicated pipelines that transform raw data into structured knowledge graphs or condensed summaries. For example, taking a large database and creating a pipeline that summarizes a million data entries into one entry every 12 hours. This way, we ensure the model receives a small, synthesized body of knowledge (1 entry point in the database) rather than a chaotic stream of consciousness (the whole database, sometimes).

Foundational models like GPT-4 and Claude, as well as vector databases like Pinecone and Milvus, have become an accessible commodity. Everyone can access them today through their services. Yet, this is not the same for context; the architectural principles for working with context are highly domain-specific. Every company should design its own context based on the business domain and the product it serves. For example, a fintech firm might choose to curate context for an autonomous fraud-analysis agent by prioritizing transaction timestamps, geolocation anomalies, and strict compliance rules. This will look entirely different for a legal tech firm. A legal tech firm might choose to curate context based on state law for use with an agent that generates contracts. We are learning that the context itself cannot be generic; it must reflect the unique domain logic, security boundaries, and vocabulary of the specific product.

Treating context as a continuous lifecycle allows us, as engineering teams, to manage knowledge systematically and directly address the root causes of model failure and prohibitive inference costs. The Lifecycle Stages

Generally speaking, there are 4 stages: Selection, Injection, Compression, Expiration & Refresh.  Figure 2 describes how each stage could be a dedicated module in our architecture or a standalone service.

Figure 2: Agentic AI Systemic Context Lifecycle (Source: created by the author with Gemini)

The first and most important step. This is where the system identifies which data points are likely to matter for the current task. The system's goal is to identify the absolute highest-value data points across multiple data stores. Advanced architectures have moved beyond simple cosine similarity in vector spaces, implementing hybrid search algorithms that combine dense semantic search with sparse keyword search (e.g., BM25) and knowledge graph traversal to ensure precision. In this process, we want to understand intent, task type, risk, user role, and temporal relevance. It is important to remember that the same underlying corpus may yield different contexts for a troubleshooting agent, a research agent, and a support summarization agent. This is where architecture begins to diverge from product. As part of the design requirements, we need to identify and define what is risky and what is actionable.

Once the system knows what matters, it has to place that information into the model’s working context (aka context window) in a useful form. While the end result might look like simple string concatenation, the path to getting there requires more deliberate design. That design involves semantic templating, ensuring the data is formatted to match the user's explicit intent, including necessary system instructions, few-shot examples, and output schema constraints (such as JSON definitions). To understand the importance of this step, consider how it affects the entire system. In our world, this placement of information changes how models reason. Hence, order, grouping, and structured state matter.

Processing a large context is expensive. To respect token limits, historical data should be iteratively compressed. Utilizing smaller, faster LLMs (or even deterministic algorithms) to summarize conversation histories or condense long documents saves massive amounts of space and reduces latency for the primary reasoning model. Test summaries carefully to avoid distortions. There are statistical models available today to assess summary validity, such as the Perplexity (PPL) Ratio, Token-Level Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, the Chi-Square Test for Categorical Outputs, and others.

Context that never expires eventually turns into a liability. Agents need mechanisms to retire stale assumptions, refresh live facts, and separate durable truths from temporary observations. A system preference might remain stable across months or change overnight. A product configuration might change in minutes. A support incident may be relevant for a day and misleading a week later. Without expiration and refresh, systems fall into stale data loops: they keep reusing context that was once correct but is now simply persuasive. Hence, constantly testing and validating the system through feedback loops is a must. This should be tailored to the system's end goal. For example, in a car-sharing system, the goal is to satisfy users; hence, if user satisfaction drops suddenly, it’s best to explore underlying factors that may need refreshing.

LLM hallucinations are rarely the result of a "broken" model; they are almost always the symptom of an unmanaged, impoverished context window. Because LLMs are probabilistic, when an agent lacks the explicit, factual data required to answer a prompt or execute a task, its underlying mechanism forces it to "guess" based on latent training weights.

Proactive context management acts as a strict guardrail. By saturating the model with highly relevant, high-confidence knowledge and explicitly instructing it to reason only based on the provided context, we can effectively suppress latent, inaccurate associations. In a productionized agentic system, a well-engineered context engine becomes our primary defense against hallucinated actions.

Processing a large context is notoriously expensive. Every token injected into the prompt window incurs both a computational latency cost and a strict financial cost. Token Economics is the engineering discipline of optimizing "attention real estate" within the LLM's limitations.

The recent expansion of context windows (e.g., models boasting 128k to 1M+ token limits) has tempted developers towards lazy architecture. They dump entire code repositories or massive troves of documents into the prompt. This drastically increases Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency, skyrockets API billing costs, and, ironically, degrades model performance. The model suffers from the "Lost in the Middle" phenomenon, shown in Figure 3. This problem was identified by Stanford researchers Nelson F. Liu et al. in 2023, where the model fails to retrieve facts buried in the center of massive context windows and only focuses on edge case information. The larger the bottom part of the U shape (context window), the less accurate the response will be. This research explains why we want the context sent to the model to be relatively small. This approach makes the U bottom part smaller as well - hence, improving outcomes.

Architects must weigh the marginal utility of every retrieved document against its token cost and relevancy. Just because we can send 100,000 tokens doesn't mean we should. Strict context budgeting, iterative pruning, and caching mechanisms are mandatory for scalable economics.

Figure 3: Lost in the middle problem - recall vs accuracy (Source: created by the author with Gemini - based on Lost in the Middle scientific paper by Stanford)

Designing systemic approaches to memory requires establishing firm boundaries for how agents retain, update, or discard knowledge across sessions. Drawing inspiration from human cognitive architecture, systems should be multi-tiered:

There are a few recurring failure patterns that show up again and again in agentic systems.

Implement Strict TTL (Time-To-Live) Policies

Not all memories are created equal. Treat agent memory like a standard caching layer by applying category-specific expiration dates.

The next generation of AI systems' success will be determined primarily by architecture design. While the industry continues to debate model parameters and raw capabilities, the core challenge for engineering teams looks remarkably familiar: state management, signal prioritization, fault isolation, data freshness, security, and cost control.

The winning architectures will treat themselves as essential infrastructure, curate context, view memory as a strict system design problem, and elevate knowledge curation to a first-class engineering discipline. This is the real shift from chatbots to autonomous agents.

#9925. Risks & Rewards: How AI Is Redefining the CISO's Role

Nvidia security executive Mark Weatherford says CISOs must help business leaders weigh AI's pros and cons, and ensure those deploying it own the risks.

ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026 — Denver — The CISO role is evolving around AI, with security leaders now expected to help the business gain a competitive edge with it while also using the technology to help manage cyber-risk.

Doing both jobs at once means keeping up with technology that changes by the month, Mark Weatherford, Nvidia's head of cybersecurity policy and strategic engagement, said this week at the ISC2 Strategic Congress 2026.

"Speed is the biggest challenge right now," Weatherford said in a conference session on the evolving CISO role in the AI era. "Technology is changing so fast it is really hard for us to keep pace."

The shift shows up in routine practices too, he noted. Penetration testing four times a year, for instance, once counted as adequate. Now, anyone not testing around the clock is probably not testing enough.

Weatherford served as deputy undersecretary for cybersecurity at DHS in the Obama administration and was previously chief information security officer for the state of Colorado and the state of California. His other career highlights include serving as chief security officer of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) and as a security leader at Booking Holdings.

Related:As AI Reshapes the SOC Career Ladder, Satisfaction Rises for 91%, but Entry Gets Harder for Nearly Half

Weatherford pointed to a sense of FOMO — or a fear of missing out — as driving many organizations to deploy AI without always doing business due diligence or understanding what value they might be deriving from their investment. While there are many instances where the rush to spend might make sense, there are other cases where the case for AI may not be as clear-cut.

CISOs often, though, have the opposite tendency, which is defaulting to "no" when there is the slightest element of risk involved. Weatherford pointed to the Navy concept of command by negation where subordinates take autonomous action to meet an overall goal unless the superior asks them to stop.

He opined that cybersecurity leaders should similarly be willing to accept more risk on their own, calibrated to their company's risk tolerance. "You have to be curious. You have to be willing to step out of your comfort zone," he said.

Weatherford encouraged CISOs to continuously think about how AI can help transform business and security and look for opportunities to make themselves better in their role. CISOs who expect their reputations and past work alone to carry them through the future are limiting their potential, he cautioned.

"Be curious, be creative, be willing to learn and relearn," Weatherford said, adding that one way to get up to speed on AI is to pick up one new topic every week.

Related:Fighting Your Dragons Through Tough Tech Times

The worry about being too slow to tap AI comes amid growing concern about organizations moving too quickly to implement AI without considering appropriate controls or without a full appreciation of associated risks, Weatherford noted. It is the role of the CISO to make sure the board understands the risks and knows who owns each risk, especially when another executive's deployment creates it.

Such frankness can potentially be career-limiting at times, Weatherford conceded. But CISOs often end up getting blamed for decisions that are not theirs, and they need to push back, he advised. "I would say we need to make sure that the people taking the risk are responsible for the risk.

For the talent pipeline, Weatherford favors paid internships that bring AI-native young people into the company and teach them the business. One of his interview ideas is to hand a candidate a business problem and let them use AI to solve it live, with no single right answer, to test flexibility.

It's also important for CISOs to ensure that people continue to have a career path and upward mobility within the organization, Weatherford said. It's a mistake to assume that paying people more and keeping them in their same roles is a way to retain talent.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9923. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9921. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

InfoQ Homepage News Uber Builds MCP Gateway to Govern Access to 800+ Servers and 5,000+ AI Agent Tools

Nov 02, 2026 2 min read

Uber has built an MCP Gateway to standardize how AI agents discover and invoke internal services, addressing fragmented integrations, duplicated infrastructure, and inconsistent security practices as agent adoption expands across the company. The platform supports more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools, providing a common layer for discovery, protocol translation, authorization, and execution.

Uber engineers describe this approach as a microservice architecture that exposes existing APIs as MCP tools without requiring changes to the underlying services. The architecture separates the MCP Registry, which acts as the control plane, from the Proxy Gateway, which handles runtime execution. The registry maintains tool definitions, schemas, ownership, and enablement settings, while the proxy translates MCP requests into HTTP, gRPC, or TChannel calls and converts responses back into MCP-compatible results.

Uber MCP Gateway with APIs as tools (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The architecture has drawn comparisons with established API gateway patterns. Ajay Sharma, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft CoreAI, wrote in a LinkedIn post,

Azure API Gateways has been doing this for a while now. It's a recipe for order to the chaos that LLMs come with.

Kelly Goetsch, President at Pipe17, similarly observed in a LinkedIn post that

Uber's new MCP gateway looks identical to gateways we've built over the decades for APIs and later GraphQL.

Tamir Dresher highlighted in a LinkedIn post the continuing relevance of established distributed systems concerns, including security, discovery, observability, and governance.

Uber’s AutoCrawler automates tool discovery using Cadence. It scans internal interface definition language (IDL) registries and extracts API definitions from Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas. It then generates MCP-compatible schemas and uses a large language model to produce tool descriptions. Newly discovered tools remain disabled until their owning teams review and explicitly enable them. Configuration changes propagate to the data plane without requiring service restarts or redeployments.

Auto Crawler Flow (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The gateway enforces authorization at both server and tool levels through Uber’s internal access control system. It also supports redaction of personally identifiable information (PII) and other sensitive data in tool responses. For third-party integrations, including Jira and Google, a separate service exchanges internal user tokens for the corresponding third-party authentication tokens.

As the tool catalog grows, loading definitions for thousands of tools into an agent’s context becomes inefficient. Uber developed Omni MCP to support incremental discovery, allowing agents to search for servers, discover relevant tools, retrieve individual schemas, and invoke selected tools as needed. Response Projection lets agents request specific response fields instead of receiving complete payloads. Uber’s aifx command-line interface also enables coding agents to discover and invoke tools, writing results to files for selective inspection.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9918. kitty 0.50.0

kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast, GPU based terminal. To update kitty, follow the instructions.

The resize page now offers two strategies: Window retains the usual width/height controls, while Edge lets you choose an internal pane edge in the Splits layout and move its divider in a physical direction.

Press H to select the middle pane’s left edge. Gray edges are outside the layout and cannot be selected.¶

After selecting H, Alt+H moves the left divider by one third of the remaining resize steps. The right divider stays in place.¶

Switch strategies with 1/2 inside the page. Each strategy remembers its own Alt/Shift modifier and fraction, configurable with M and F. A sole internal edge is selected automatically. In Splits, either strategy uses R to restore the proportions saved when resize mode opened. See Resizing windows for the controls and configuration options.

kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders. These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised.

See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty.

This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details:

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths

Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+).

Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD, filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images

Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives.

Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped

kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows.

kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program.

kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for smooth scrolling and momentum based scrolling for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience.

Additionally, you can now drag kitty tabs around with the mouse to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into their own OS Window.

Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented.

A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text.

On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs.

kitty has long had support for Sessions, aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file, for seamless and intuitive session file creation.

A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is extensively configurable in kitty.conf. Note that the old scrollback_indicator_opacity option is deprecated.

kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last.

kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress.

See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up.

kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol.

Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be turned on by the cursor_trail option in kitty.conf.

Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports OpenType Variable fonts. These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization abilities, such as: symbol_map, text_composition_strategy, font_features and modify_font. kitty knows text rendering is important, and goes the extra mile for it.

kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features.

Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements:

Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background

Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol

The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically

kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor

With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor.

Allow docking kitty windows to the edges of other windows or of the tab, for status bars, file trees, etc. Create them with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock, see Docked windows

A new option restore_session_after_logout to save the state of every kitty instance, including scrollback, when logging out, restarting or shutting down and restore it the next time kitty starts. On macOS, the state is encrypted with a key in the keychain. On Linux, it requires the Inhibit desktop portal. See Restoring kitty after logging out (#1197, #10659)

Allow using tabs like named workspaces: A new launch --focus-existing option to focus an existing window or tab instead of creating a new one, a new by-title value for launch --location to keep tabs in alphabetical order and new options for kitten @ detach-window and the detach_window action to send windows to a named tab, creating it if needed (#10627)

Wayland: The client side window decorations used on compositors such as GNOME now look like native GNOME decorations and follow the desktop titlebar font, text scaling, button layout and titlebar click action settings (#10766)

Wayland: Support touchscreens. A tap is a click, a finger that moves scrolls with momentum, and a finger held still before it moves selects text (#5432, #10551)

Custom shaders: New cursor-trail-railgun, cursor-trail-torpedo and cursor-trail-pixiedust shaders that make particles fly off the cursor as it moves, in the style of neovide. Shaders can now be controlled with key presses via the new shader_event action (see Controlling shaders with key presses), can be faded in and out, reversed and looped with new animation_* pipeline directives and can define a pointer_map() function so that clicks and selections land on the text shown under the mouse, which the crt shader now uses, see Shaders that move content. Also fix animations becoming jerky after kitty has been running for a few hours, shaders specified by path not being found and various pipeline bugs (#10587, #10667, #10693, #10595, #10694, #10639)

Graphics protocol: Add two new indexed color image formats whose pixels are indices into the terminal color palette, so that images change color along with the color scheme, and allow clients to detect support for individual protocol features, such as animation and Unicode placeholders, via the new e query key, see Querying support for protocol features (#9379, #10732)

Support the Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) that lets programs report whether they are working, finished, failed or blocked waiting on the user. Shown in the tab bar via a new tab.program_status field for tab_title_template, see Reporting the status of a program

Automatic color themes: When the system switches between light and dark, keep colors set by programs running in a window, by the ssh kitten, by launch --color or launch --copy-colors, and use the current theme colors when a program restores its saved colors. launch --color colors now also survive config reloads. The ssh kitten can use different color schemes for remote hosts in dark and light mode via the new kitten-ssh.color_scheme_dark, kitten-ssh.color_scheme_light and kitten-ssh.color_scheme_no_preference options (#10724)

Layouts: Align the borders of neighboring windows and keep the gaps between them uniform, and add a new option collapse_window_margins to have the margins of neighboring windows collapse into each other instead of adding up (#10508)

Window resizing: A new --strategy=edge mode to select and move a specific internal divider in the Splits layout, and hold Alt with a resize letter to take a fraction of the remaining resize steps, configurable with the new --fraction option

Scale the thickness of box drawing characters, cursors and the window title bar border with the font size, so they no longer look too thin when zoomed in or too thick when zoomed out. At the configured font_size nothing changes (#10362)

mouse_map can now map the scroll wheel, via the wheel_up, wheel_down, wheel_left and wheel_right buttons, for example, to change the font size with Ctrl+scroll

A new option hyperlink_target_position to control where the URL shown by show_hyperlink_targets is displayed, including as a browser style tooltip next to the mouse cursor (#10770)

Show the hand pointer and hover highlighting over links only when the pressed modifiers match a configured mouse action for opening the link with a single click, updating immediately when modifiers are pressed or released

quick-access-terminal kitten: New kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --if-running, kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --listen-on and kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --hold options to run programs in an already running quick access terminal, use a fixed remote control socket and keep the terminal open after the program exits (#10603)

Sessions: A new os_window_position keyword and a new --os-window-geometry option for save_as_session to save the size, position and state of OS Windows in session files. Also fix the OS Window size and os_window_title in sessions sometimes being ignored (#10675)

Command palette: Show action and kitten aliases at the top when the search query is empty, so they can be used to pin frequently used actions (#10711)

Vertical tab bars: When tab_title_max_length is set, size the tab bar to fit the decorations of the current tab_bar_style, allowing much narrower tab bars (#10680)

Linux/BSD: Detect MIME types for open actions and kittens using the shared-mime-info cache, matching the rest of the desktop, including files without an extension, such as Makefile, and MIME type aliases (#3056)

IME: Keep the candidate window anchored at the start of the pre-edit text and at the cursor, so it no longer jumps around while composing text. On macOS, commit in-progress IME or dictation text instead of discarding it when the OS window loses focus (#10642, #10644)

Shell integration: Make the kitty terminfo files available in commands run via run0, similar to sudo (#10692)

kitty --config=NONE now also skips the automatic color theme files, open-actions.conf, launch-actions.conf, mime.types, paste-actions.py, notifications.py and the custom window icon in the kitty config directory

Processes kitty inserts to wrap the program it runs, such as /usr/bin/login on macOS or the wrapper for launch --hold, are now skipped when reporting the pid, working directory, command line and environment of a window in kitten @ ls and when matching windows. Also fix launch --cwd=root using the working directory of the foreground process instead of the root process while the shell is running a command

Nightly builds now show the date and hash of the commit they were built from in the output of kitty --version and kitten --version

Do not render between render frames to reduce flicker from programs that draw with many small partial updates (#10749)

Performance: Faster growing of the GPU sprite cache, particularly on macOS, less CPU usage with a non-zero input_delay and no continuous re-rendering when a selection is present and the window is scrolled back (#10714)

Remote control: Fix a crafted request being able to bypass password based remote control authentication by masquerading as a cancellation of an asynchronous request

Remote control: Fix many commands, including action, send-key, set-colors, set-background-opacity, set-font-size, ls, run and set-enabled-layouts, ignoring options, reporting false success or silently misinterpreting invalid input, particularly when used in remote_control mappings. set-colors now parses color files the same way as kitty.conf. Also fix a single unresponsive peer blocking all remote control communication and a crash when using damaged images with set-window-logo or set-background-image (#10672, #10632, #10688, #10690, #10715)

Fix various terminal emulation bugs, including in origin mode cursor position reports, erasing multicell characters, the CHT escape code and copying text containing tabs, wide characters being drawn on the wrong row after colliding with scaled text, emoji sequences being split into multiple cells when wrapped, text typed into a new window before the program is ready sometimes being garbled, as well as a heap buffer overflow, an out of bounds write and a use-after-free when reloading the config (#10609, #10729, #10632, #10682, #10767)

Graphics protocol: Allow shared memory object names without a leading slash again, for sandboxed macOS applications, and fix various bugs with animation frames and Unicode placeholders (#10684, #10599, #10632)

Fix various window and tab management bugs, with focus moving to the wrong window on close, drag and drop onto title bars, visual window selection, Grid layout placement, title bar padding and tab titles being truncated too early. detach_tab now shows custom titles in the OS Window chooser (#10640)

Fix render jitter when scrolled back with a partial line and the client is using the synchronised rendering escape code (#10794)

Fix bold or italic Nerd Font icons sometimes being rendered using glyphs from an unrelated font, the cursor trail not always being shown when focus moves to a different window, watcher entries not being removed on config reload and changing text marker colors at runtime, for example with kitten @ set-colors or automatic theme switching, applying the colors of each marker to the next one (#10591)

ssh kitten: Preserve the permissions of copied directories, fix copying files outside HOME whose paths share its prefix and files in HOME being copied to an absolute path with --symlink-strategy=resolve when HOME is a symlink, fix hanging when re-using a shared connection that has silently died and fix colors 16-255 being set to white with themes that do not define them (#10691, #10661, #10727, #10737)

Desktop UI kitten: Fix D-Bus activation when kitten is installed in a path containing spaces or quoting characters (#10784)

Automatic color themes: Stop using cached colors and background images after the corresponding theme file has been deleted and apply theme files created after kitty was started when reloading the config (#10786)

Themes kitten: Fix overwriting the Unicode input kitten’s recent entries and input mode, and vice versa, by using separate caches (#10780)

Remote file kitten: Preserve the local edited copy and show its recovery path when the final upload fails, including when the SSH connection has died (#10789)

Transfer kitten: When receiving files, replace existing symbolic and hard links at the destination instead of overwriting the files they point to, and write to a temporary file that is renamed into place, so an interrupted transfer no longer leaves a truncated file behind (#10713)

Drag and drop kitten: Reject copying or moving a directory into itself or one of its subdirectories, and moving a directory into a symlink that points inside it, which would delete the moved files. When moving, do not delete sources that were replaced during the drop, for example by files merged through a symlink in the destination. Respect overwrite confirmation for case and Unicode equivalent names on filesystems that treat them as aliases, list the existing files that will be overwritten under their actual names, including inside symlinked directories, and fix dropping a directory over an existing file. No longer rename remotely dropped files whose names differ only in case on case sensitive filesystems (#10769, #10772)

Drag and drop protocol: Fix base64 data with padding at the end being rejected, as allowed by the protocol (#10777)

Clipboard kitten: Fix only the last of several outputs that use the same MIME type being saved, for example with kitten clipboard -g picture.png picture.jpg, the data is now downloaded and decoded only once for all such outputs. Reject duplicate output files, including ones that differ only in case on case-insensitive filesystems or whose paths contain a symlink followed by ... Fix a race when replacing an existing output file, losing the original file if writing it fails and kitten clipboard -g -m . formats.txt silently doing nothing. Also preserve the permissions of and follow symlinks at existing output files (#10738, #10744)

Kittens: When saving files, such as themes, config files or clipboard output, write to the target of a symlink even when the target does not yet exist, instead of replacing the symlink with a regular file (#10740)

Kittens: Fix laggy mouse selection and failures comparing remote directories in the diff kitten, Unicode quotes not being removed from around paths and URLs in the hints kitten, the order of styles with negative or closely spaced fractional axis values in the choose-fonts kitten, various bugs in the choose-files, quick-access-terminal and other kittens and reject command-line options missing their required value (#10634, #10641, #10676, #10687, #10730)

Wayland: Fix a crash on compositors without cursor-shape support, kitty being disconnected by GNOME when showing a long covered window, the app_id being lost when hiding and showing windows, kitty --os-window-tag not setting the window tag and various drag and drop bugs (#10597, #10602, #10604, #10759, #10632)

Linux: Fix momentum scrolling up or left, X11 wheel events from sources without smooth scrolling being ignored and various desktop notification bugs. Notifications now identify kitty’s desktop file, so desktops such as KDE can group them (#10625, #10695, #10610, #10721)

macOS: Fix padding rendering black after sleep, OS windows not staying on all spaces, a duplicate path when dropping items from Apple Mail, emoji from a monochrome emoji font such as Noto Emoji not using the foreground color, a memory leak, reloading config causing Apple injected shortcuts to not work and kitty freezing when opening a new window while another entry in /dev is stuck (#10708, #10581, #10628, #10673, #10741, #10757, #10793)

zsh: Respect the user’s descriptions format style for completion group headings, fixing literal %B markers appearing with fzf-tab, and fix a “maximum nested function level reached” error at every prompt after interrupting a command run at shell startup, for example via a session file (#10748, #10768)

Fix reverse-video extra cursors to use the color type encoded by the multiple-cursors protocol.
