#9843. Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

The pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

The “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Issues and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗

Compare and rank TTS voice models with blind A/B voting

Explore speech model performance across datasets

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS."

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let users listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard

#9841. Finchb Opens a Help Center as Solana Bird Passes 7,000 Players

The Solana wallet for the web and Telegram explains the app, its products, and exchanging coins in nine languages, adds video tutorials on YouTube and repeats its safety rules.

Finchb, a wallet for the Solana blockchain that runs in the browser, as an installable app and inside Telegram, has opened

a help center at www.finchb.com/help. In 20 articles and nine languages, it explains how the app works, how its products are used and how to exchange coins with the wallet. Inside Telegram, the wallet runs through the Finchb bot, @finchb_bot.

The help center walks through the wallet step by step: signing in, getting back in after losing access, paying in by card, sending to an exchange on the Solana network, choosing the right network, and checking a transaction on the public explorer.

Exchanging has its own answers. Coins from other networks, such as USDT, TON, or BTC, can be paid in and arrive in the wallet as USDC, with the swap partner SideShift doing the exchange, and SOL can be swapped out to another network, for example as USDT on TRON. The screen shows what arrives before the customer confirms.

For the products of the wallet, the help center explains the fees of Solana Bird, Meme Radar and Grid Bot and how their payouts reach the wallet: a Grid Bot withdrawal with one tap, a Meme Radar package paid out by itself at the end of its term, and the Solana Bird balance moved over to the wallet. When a customer pays USDC into Solana Bird or Meme Radar without holding SOL, Finchb covers the network fee.

Each answer lists the steps; the most-asked ones show the real app screen, and where an action costs something, the fee is stated. The articles were written by the Finchb team with AI assistance and checked against the live app.

Finchb’s YouTube channel now has step-by-step videos in English: a one-minute tour of the wallet, creating a wallet, installing the app on iPhone and Android, a first deposit, and buying SOL or USDC with a card, each as a full video and as a Short.

Solana Bird, a flying game inside the wallet, has passed 7,000 players in its first month. Payouts from the products of the wallet are public: the first Meme Radar packages have been paid out to customers since late October, Grid Bot withdrawals have run since mid-October,

and every product payout appears in a public Telegram channel with its transaction on the Solana blockchain.

The public payouts page: every payout fromthe Finchb products is listed with its transaction on Solana.

Customers can also share a personal link through the Finchb Partner program and receive a share of the purchases made by

With a growing community, Finchb repeats its safety rules. The team never sends the first private message and never asks for the 12 recovery words, and on Telegram Finchb writes to users only through its official bot. Finchb recommends securing every account with a confirmed email address, a password and two-factor authentication.

“Every customer should find the answer in the app’s own words and in their own language: how the wallet works, how each product is used and how to exchange coins. The videos show the same steps on screen, and our safety rules stay simple: the team never writes first and never asks for recovery words,” said the Finchb team.

Finchb is a wallet for the Solana blockchain that runs on the web, as an installable app on phones and computers, and inside Telegram. A new wallet is created with one tap and without an email address. Finchb is based in Singapore.

#9840. Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

As artificial intelligence squeezes early-career learning opportunities, capture-the-flag contests could be one way to help pick up the slack.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may be gobbling up entry-level jobs and learning opportunities for security practitioners, but it can't erase the value of hands-on experience with enterprise systems and security tools.

No matter how much agentic action cybersecurity teams embed into their security operations center (SOC) and the rest of their programs, smart people have to backstop that work. And the only way these "humans-in-the-loop" can do that capably is if they build up the kind of judgment that's best learned from the school of hard knocks.

The problem? With SOC tier 1 analysts becoming an endangered species and bug bounty programs on the ropes from a glut of AI submissions, the chances are dwindling for security newbies to rack up real-world experience.

There's no great fix to this career pipeline problem just yet, but some of the answers might be found in one of the industry's age-old mechanisms for both camaraderie and skill-building: the trusty capture-the-flag (CTF) competition.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"CTFs give passionate talent the opportunity to grow and learn in ways that they might not have at their day jobs," says Jason Walker, a security engineer by day at software-as-a-service firm Five9. An avid CTF competitor, he won the Sentinels League competition sponsored and run by SentinelOne, beating two other finalists from a field of thousands of competitors worldwide. Besides street cred, Walker picked up a $5,000 prize for his efforts and a $10,000 donation in his name to his charity of choice, Trans Lifeline.

The livestreamed event offered up the spectacle and fun of an e-sports competition, but it may hold deeper clues as to how the industry can keep refreshing its talent pool in the coming years. As Walker puts it, CTFs are the ultimate way to expose both new and experienced cyber professionals to a wider range of problems and technologies.

"CTFs have helped me be a lot more versatile," he says. "If your company is running well and your program is mature, you aren't going to necessarily be firefighting new things every week. You're not going to be exposed to every new technique and threat. Doing CTF events and other hands-on training is a really important way to make sure you can stay up to date."

CTF competitions come in many shapes and sizes, but they fundamentally challenge players to find hidden pieces of data called "flags" buried inside intentionally vulnerable systems. Most fall into one of two formats: Jeopardy-style events, the kind Sentinels League runs, hand out standalone puzzles across categories such as Web exploitation, forensics, and cryptography, with points awarded per solve. Attack-defense events ask each team to defend its own vulnerable network while trying to break into everyone else's.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

The attack-defense format took shape at DEF CON's CTF, which started in 1996 and is still the event most associated with it. It has sprung forth a wellspring of CTF formats that range from grassroots industry events to big vendor-sponsored competitions like Sentinels League.

Sentinels League grew out of ThreatOps, a set of internal games SentinelOne's solutions engineers have run since 2020 to teach customers how to hunt through telemetry for hidden flags. This year's championship built on that with four games — Endpoint, Cloud, SIEM, and AI — spread across 12 weeks of qualifiers between June and October

The opening player pool of 2,236 entrants came from more than 100 countries, competing for a total prize pool of $100,000. Smaller prizes were dispensed across the qualifier and regional events, with the bigger prizes kept on reserve for the final, which was held in conjunction with SentinelOne's annual OneCon event.

Ryan O'Grady, director of SE operations at SentinelOne, says the firm invests the money in the prizes and the considerable logistics of running such a big event as a way to give back to the community, to build up expertise and exposure to its platform, and as a recruiting tool.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

Whether motivated for the prizes or the training, the appetite for the event keeps growing. This year's drew enough interest that the company had to get a bigger ballroom to accommodate spectators.

Sentinels League is just one example of what a CTF looks like amid a much broader spectrum of competitions available. On CTFtime, the volunteer-run archive that tracks the hobbyist side of the scene, last year's calendar alone listed more than 200 individually organized events, with active teams from countries spanning every populated continent.

DEF CON CTF, often called the World Series of hacking, pulled 673 teams through its 2026 qualifiers before finals in Las Vegas this August. The National Cyber League, a nonprofit circuit O'Grady competes in, drew more than 7,500 students from 670 schools and universities this past spring. Kaspersky continues to run its own wildly popular SAS CTF out of Bali.

Other more academic events, such as New York University's CSAW and Carnegie Mellon's picoCTF, run versions aimed at students. Larger consulting firms, such as KPMG, use the format to scout corporate recruits.

In spite of the obvious demand for CTFs evident in the number of events held worldwide and the thousands of participants willing to sink their personal time into these pursuits, many security pundits worry about what AI is going to do to the purpose and purity of these competitions.

CTF organizers are thinking deeply about what this means for their rule books and how they enforce them. RITSEC's 2026 rules ban using AI to autonomously solve challenges outright, calling it against the spirit of the competition. Meantime, CSAW leaned into AI, this year creating an entire track built around using large language models (LLMs) to solve past CTF problems.

DEF CON CTF's 2026 qualifier split the difference. It barred fully autonomous AI teams but let human competitors use AI tools as long as a person stayed meaningfully in charge, requiring every team to label itself No AI, Low AI, or Human-Led AI on the public scoreboard.

A recent study of hundreds of Hack The Box machines released between 2017 and 2025 found solve times dropped roughly 16% a year, with the steepest declines after 2022. The hardest tier of challenges went from a 15-hour median solve down to about five, according to penetration tester Jacob Krell of Suzu Labs, who did the analysis.

He's not the only one worried. An academic study earlier this year from IBM Research and the College of William & Mary pitted 41 participants in a live, on-site CTF against four autonomous AI agents. It found that those agents placed second overall, ahead of most of the human teams competing.

Findings like these are enough to get firms like OtterSec, a blockchain security firm, to make noise about how to "save" CTFs. This summer the firm launched a $100,000 "Save CTFs Fund" to bankroll new formats that stay meaningful as AI keeps improving.

SentinelOne's O'Grady doesn't buy the death-of-CTFs talk. In his view, AI just forces organizers to redesign CTFs so they still force a human to think laterally, AI assistance or not.

AI may not be killing creative CTFs anytime soon, but it is definitely making cybersecurity's career ladder wobble. In the process it may actually be making CTFs even more crucial.

SANS Institute polled nearly 1,000 security leaders and found unclear career progression to be one of the top hiring challenges, cited by 32%, more than triple the rate last year. Only one-quarter of organizations say they have a clearly defined career path, and entry-level jobs that used to train the next generation of defenders are diminishing. SOC and security analyst roles lead the AI-driven cuts, down 32%. Threat intelligence analysts are next, at 26%, with incident responders close behind, at 22%.

Bug bounty programs are buckling under AI's pressure. At the start of the year, maintainers of the open source project Curl shut down their program after a massive influx of junk AI submissions. HackerOne paused its Internet Bug Bounty program in April after a wave of low-quality, AI-assisted reports flooded in. And this month Google Bug Hunters also paused its open source bounty program due to similar problems.

These are all blows for cyber career progression, as bug bounty problems were another great place for security professionals to flex their skills publicly and for newcomers to gain a foothold into the industry.

As long as CTF organizers can keep their competitions relevant, these events will remain a valuable puzzle piece in the skills training picture for the industry, alongside other important hands-on challenges like cyber ranges.

"With LLMs basically sweeping the table on bug bounties, it's become even harder than it already was for people to get out there, show off their skills, and get their name out there," O'Grady says. "AI has only increased the importance of CTF events like this."

#9839. AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

Enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates new tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

The specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little new training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

For example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:

A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:

The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

#9838. Personalization Without Creepiness: Design AI Marketing Around Permissions

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A CRM contains enough context to make a message feel personal. That does not mean every available detail belongs in the message. An internal support issue, an old sales note, or an inferred interest can make outreach seem informed while violating the recipient's expectations.

The engineering challenge is to decide which context may influence an action, for what purpose, and under whose authority. Personalization is not just a generation problem. It is a sequence of access, purpose, eligibility, and approval decisions.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would build those decisions into the workflow before expanding personalization. The framework below is a technical design proposal, not jurisdiction-specific legal advice or a claim that a CRM field establishes every permission required for external communication. Policy and legal questions belong with the organization's qualified owners.

Define why the message should exist. Is it responding to a request, explaining an agreed service, inviting someone to an optional event, or introducing a relevant topic? The purpose should be understandable without referring to the amount of data available.

For a hypothetical implementation partner, a customer asking about a workflow may need a scoped technical answer. That does not justify inserting unrelated details from another department's notes. A relevant answer can be specific without displaying everything the company knows about the person.

Write a short purpose statement for each workflow. Use it to decide which data is necessary and which actions are appropriate. If the purpose cannot be explained clearly, pause the automation design rather than asking the model to discover a persuasive reason after retrieving the record.

Access asks whether the system may read the data. Purpose asks whether the data should be used for this task. Eligibility asks whether this recipient and relationship qualify for the proposed action under the approved policy. Approval asks whether the actual message is authorized for release.

Passing one gate does not pass the others. A user may have technical access to a contact record while lacking authority to publish its contents. A recipient may be eligible for one type of communication but not another. An approved template may still produce an inappropriate individual message.

Keep the gates explicit in implementation and reporting. A generated draft should not be treated as approved because retrieval succeeded. An approval should be scoped to the recipient-visible state, not merely to the general intention to use personalization.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A broad record export is convenient for a model and difficult for a reviewer to reason about. Reduce the context to the facts necessary for the stated purpose. Where possible, exclude unrelated notes and sensitive material before generation rather than relying only on an instruction not to mention them.

For example, a reminder about an agreed technical workshop might need the workshop topic, approved participants, relevant date, and a link to the preparation material. It does not need a complete history of every ticket or an inferred personal profile.

HubSpot's AI-settings documentation describes feature and data-source controls. Treat those as configuration boundaries, not as substitutes for task-specific data selection. Confirm what the actual account permits and what the approved workflow requires before enabling a broader source.

A person's explicit request, a verified business role, and a model's guess about their priorities are different forms of context. Preserve the difference in the research record and avoid presenting an inference as something the recipient has told you.

A company announcement may justify investigating a topic. It does not prove a particular employee owns the resulting project. An old page visit may indicate interest, accidental navigation, or a colleague using the same environment. The available signal should not become a confident claim about internal plans.

Use modest language when the evidence is limited, or omit the personalization entirely. A useful message about a relevant problem can be better than a superficially personal introduction built on uncertain facts. The aim is relevance with defensible context, not a demonstration of surveillance.

Reviewers need to know why a factual statement appears in a draft. That does not mean the recipient should see internal notes or confidential source references. Keep an internal evidence envelope separate from the public-facing message.

The W3C provenance overview describes origins and transformations. An application-specific evidence envelope could record the source reference, supported statement, date checked, permitted use, and unresolved uncertainty. These are proposed fields, not a native marketing audit schema.

Protect the evidence record according to its sensitivity. Do not copy private customer information into ordinary campaign URLs, public prompts, or broadly shared spreadsheets. If the workflow cannot keep the internal evidence separate from the outward artifact, simplify the workflow before expanding its reach.

A recipient's status can change between research and release. Ownership may change, a suppression may be added, a relationship may end, or the intended sender's connection may become unavailable. A decision captured days earlier should not be assumed current forever.

Define which checks must be refreshed immediately before the consequential action. Use supported product controls and the organization's approved policy. If a required check is unavailable or contradictory, hold the item with an owner and a reason rather than selecting the most convenient value.

This is not a claim that every marketing platform exposes the same controls. Test the actual configuration. If an automatic workflow cannot enforce an important boundary, retain a manual release gate or choose a narrower use case. Technical convenience does not eliminate the missing requirement.

The sender changes how a message is understood. A note from an account owner can imply a relationship that the same words from a general mailbox would not. A fallback sender may keep an automation moving while introducing a misleading interpersonal context.

Define which senders are appropriate for each workflow and how exceptions are handled. Test missing owners, disconnected inboxes, ownership changes, and shared accounts. Do not let a model choose a person merely because that person's name makes the introduction more persuasive.

Keep reply ownership explicit. A personalized message creates an expectation that someone can understand and respond to the context it references. If the receiving team cannot support that conversation, the system is producing a relationship promise the organization may not be ready to fulfill.

HubSpot's Prospecting Agent documentation describes reviewed and autonomous outreach modes. A product's ability to execute an action does not decide an organization's authorization policy.

For a review-first deployment, inspect the complete final message: sender, recipients, subject, body, links, formatting, and attachments. Make approval invalid when a material recipient-visible field changes. A general instruction to prepare outreach should not silently become permission to send every generated version.

Also separate approved, scheduled, sent-confirmed, and delivered where the owning system exposes those states. An enrollment or draft record proves neither a successful send nor a recipient response. Reporting should reflect the actual evidence, particularly when the workflow crosses several tools.

Create synthetic fixtures that include an unrelated support incident, an uncertain role, an outdated company announcement, a private note, an ambiguous preference, and a changed relationship status. Define which facts the draft may use and which must be excluded.

Review tone and implication as well as literal disclosure. A message can avoid quoting a private note while still revealing that the sender knows about a sensitive event. Ask whether a recipient would reasonably understand how the company came to use the detail.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a general risk-management basis. These proposed tests remain limited to the chosen cases. They do not prove legal compliance or eliminate the need for qualified review of the actual data and communication policy.

A hold should identify why the action stopped, who can resolve it, and what evidence is needed. Missing role verification, unclear permitted use, sender uncertainty, and a failed preference check are different problems. A generic failed state encourages blind retries.

Track the rate and causes of holds to improve upstream data and policy. If the same ambiguity occurs repeatedly, clarify the eligibility rule or narrow the workflow. Do not weaken the rule merely to increase the number of messages released.

A successful outcome may be a deliberately generic message or no message at all. The system should recognize restraint as a valid decision, not an error to overcome. Personalization is optional; respecting the relationship and the evidence is not an optional finishing step.

Reverting a prompt can stop a mistake from appearing in future drafts. It does not recall a message already sent. A recovery plan should distinguish pending work from completed external actions and identify who can review the consequence.

If a factual error reaches a recipient, preserve the exact outward message and the evidence used to create it. Stop affected pending items through supported controls. Assess whether a correction is necessary under the organization's process, and obtain separate approval for any corrective communication. Do not let an automated repair send a second unreviewed message in an attempt to fix the first.

Track the scope of the incident without expanding access unnecessarily. The relevant question may be which approved claim or workflow revision affected which messages, not a broad export of the entire customer database. Keep private evidence in its approved system and share only what the review requires.

This recovery design also improves initial implementation. It forces the team to retain source references, configuration identity, approval evidence, and owning-system outcomes. If the system cannot explain what it already did, giving it more personal context will make support harder rather than make the relationship more trustworthy.

The practical test is whether the team can explain why the recipient received this message, why these facts were used, why this sender was appropriate, and who approved the final version. The explanation should remain defensible when examined outside the campaign dashboard.

Begin with one narrow purpose and synthetic data. Add real context only through approved access and handling processes. Inspect exceptions, verify the release boundary, and expand only when the organization can support the resulting relationship.

AI marketing does not become better simply by revealing more context. It becomes better when context improves the recipient's experience without exceeding purpose, eligibility, or authority. Build those boundaries first, then decide how much personalization the message actually needs.

For a related evidence boundary, see Designing a Claim-Validation Workflow for AI-Generated Customer Emails. The framework above addresses a distinct marketing decision rather than repeating that model.

Sources checked October 21, 2026. All examples are hypothetical. No private contact records were accessed and no messages were sent.

The Case for Ungating Your Most Useful B2B Content

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

#9836. Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series discusses some of the trends and topics from Cybersecurity Awareness Month, from using AI for better training to educating next-generation workforces on modern risks and emerging threats.

AI is changing the concept of cybersecurity awareness in more ways than one.

In the latest installment of our monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea, and Dark Reading's Rob Wright discuss some of the trends they've observed during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which has shifted during the AI era with the emergence of news threats as well as revamped defense strategies.

As we’ve seen in years past, cybersecurity awareness training often becomes a compliance checkbox exercise rather than a vehicle to educate employees and users on the latest threats. And unfortunately, the threat landscape today is changing at a frenetic pace. Threat actors are taking advantage of AI tools and platforms to accelerate, enhance, and scale their attacks, whether it's social engineering schemes or wide-ranging supply chain compromises.

Thankfully, as the editors explain, some organizations are updating their programs to take more specific, line-of-business approaches for training while also accounting for the evolving threats related to AI; some programs are even using AI to create more convincing phishing simulations. Meanwhile, several US colleges and universities have increased their education offerings for AI security.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

The editors discuss these topics and more in this Reporters' Notebook episode.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright, senior news director at Dark Reading, and welcome to another edition of the Reporter's Notebook. I am here with Sharon and Eric. Would you guys like to introduce yourselves and then we'll get into the topics for today?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Sharon Shea: Hey, I am Sharon Shea. I'm the lead editor on Tech Target Cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity Dive's Eric Geller: And I'm Eric Geller. I'm a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive.

DR's Rob Wright: And this month is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. Yay! I know it's our favorite time of the year, right? We've written a fair amount of content on this topic over the last few weeks. We're still in it. We've still got about a week to go. It's not been a great run recently. There's been a lot going on, a lot of attacks, a lot of threats, a lot of urgent stuff going on in cybersecurity. But we wanted to get into some of those things here in this video discussion. Sharon, do you want to kick us off?

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah, so I will kind of take it back to the human side of Cybersecurity Awareness Month and then we can jump into some of the attack stuff later. But you know, one of the big things in Cybersecurity Awareness Month is making sure that your training programs are up to par. And granted, it's not just this month, just like Earth Day is not just one day for the Earth. We want it to be year-round.

But it does kind of give a springboard, as we called it in one of our articles, to further focus on cybersecurity throughout the year and bring a renewed focus for this month. And one report I was reading, a SANS report, said that 19% of organizations have cybersecurity awareness training programs designed primarily to meet a specific compliance or audit requirement. And that's kind of a bad way to look at things, just doing this for compliance.

Obviously, you want to do it to be secure all the time. And, you know, we all probably groan when those awareness trainings come into our inboxes every couple months or a couple times a year. They can be boring and you just click through them just to get through them and do the checkbox. But sometimes those aren't quite as effective as they should be, as we've seen. Really, you don't want to treat it as a check space, compliance checkbox exercise.

Related:As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

And one major thing that we learned from our reporting, or I think we've known for years, but it's not one size fits all, right? You really want to identify the behaviors within your organization that create risk. You want to map those threats to business consequences, establish baselines, and monitor for deviations from those.

Threat s like deepfakes trying to get into your help desk and reset MFA or, you know, the common Arup example of the CFO who was on a call with an employee and wanted them to wire a ton of money to them. And you know, you really have to focus those down on what departments really need specific trainings. I guess within the organization, you have so many different types of people to cover. You have your general employees, you have C-level, privileged admins, HR recruiting, customer-facing employees, and you have third parties, contractors, and you want to match the awareness to those sorts of risks.

I guess another thing that we can talk about too is updating the program regularly. You do want to talk about older tech. We all know that phishing is a major thing, right? It's still a problem, but you also want to talk about the newer tech — AI. And not just AI — GenAI, agentic AI, you know, all these newest technologies from the past couple of years. People know how to securely use them as well as preventing their inherent security issues.

And another thing I thought was kind of cool that we've covered is using AI in your awareness programs. We were talking to one CISO who uses phishing — I'm sorry, uses phishing simulations created by AI to personalize them for their employees, which you know is pretty cool, too. It's not just that generic boring watching the same old video from, you know, the 1900s, probably.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Yeah. You know, so kind of to solve some of the problems too of those boring programs. One of our sources, Kevin Walker of Black Swan, told Alissa Irei that you know, you really want to do short training sprints versus real world marathons. Those hour-long trainings, no one's going to get them. You know, they're not gonna pay attention throughout this whole thing. So make them highly relevant, personalized, and you really want to have those short, easy-to-consume bits that are good for your employees.

I guess talking about specific threats towards specific employees, Rob, you had an example that you guys have been covering on Dark Reading lately.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, there's a lot going on lately with AI-themed attacks. And one of the things I've noticed — we covered this a couple, a few times actually — is that there's a lot of SEO poisoning and malvertising. I think we think of like malvertising and threats like that as kind of like low-hanging fruit, kind of the type of attacks that aren't very sophisticated and that don't go very far. Maybe you get like some malware on your system from a flash ad or like a comb-over ad or something like that.

And we're finding that these ads are getting a lot more — I hate using the word sophisticated, I hate it so much, it's so overused — they're getting more effective. There's not a lot of ad blockers that are going to get you around ads on Facebook and Meta, for example. And there was a recent report from Gen Digital — well, I think it was almost a year now — that they found that one out of every three ads on Instagram and Facebook was malicious. It either pointed to malware or some type of phishing link, or it was a scam, like an outright scam.

And what's happening these days is that attackers know that they can use sponsored links and they can use these types of ads, not just your conventional like pop-up ads and stuff like that, which a lot of people do block. But they can use those sponsored links, you can use Google ads, you can use really effective SEO poisoning techniques to put stuff out like, 'Hey, download Claude Code' or something like that, or like a new AI tool.

And there are so many people out there looking for these tools right now. There are so many people, there's so much shadow AI that it's just easy to come across one of these malicious links, whether you're actively looking for it or you're just playing around — who knows? And they're hosted on legitimate infrastructure, they're hosted on — there was a report recently that Any.Run had, there were some stats about how many attacks, AI-themed attacks, are being deployed and there was a report about just massive use of Cloudflare Pages as infrastructure so it looks legitimate and then there's also like OpenAI Custom GPTs and that like that just it just looks legitimate because it's on like a real provider like it's on OpenAI or it's on Cloudflare.

And it's very easy to get tripped up by these things and click on something and then immediately download an infostealer that gets your credentials. And if you're a developer, there's been so many attacks on developers. And it's just bad news for an organization. So I think one of the things that companies ought to focus on right now is just trying to get people within the organization — obviously it depends on like what your privilege level is and where you are in the organization — but really for any type of employee that's out there looking for an AI tool, you've got to know the risk. You have to know that a lot of the stuff that you're going to be digging up out there, if it's not through an official app store of for an official channel, it very well likely could be a scam or some type of social engineering scheme that's going to drop an infostealer or something worse on your system. So that was kind of an eye opener for us.

Scary stuff. And we're not even to Halloween, so we'll see. Eric, what have you been seeing?

CD's Eric Geller: Well, I looked at things from the perspective of the next generation workforce. We're talking a lot about educating the workforces of today and trying to mitigate the threats of today. But we're also seeing a lot of change in the AI landscape that it's been difficult for the current workforce to get their heads around. So I kind of focused on preparing the next workforce to understand not only AI, but also how to guard against threats related to AI.

So, how to be an AI security practitioner, how to focus on AI security governance and risk management. And I looked at the university level to understand what kinds of courses exist out there to prepare students for careers in this area. It's no surprise that there's a lot of AI curriculum at the higher education level. What might be more of a surprise is that universities have actually gotten pretty good over the past few years at recognizing that there needs to be a security component to that work.

So I spoke to people at a number of schools that have tried to build or begin building curricula around AI security. Spoke to folks at Carnegie Mellon. They have a certificate program in AI security that's designed for kind of mid-level corporate workers who want to specialize in this area to go in for a class. It's a few weeks, you come out with a certificate that can kind of prepare you to be a leader in this space. But of course, a lot of this is happening at the undergraduate and graduate level. And so there's a lot of courses designed to kind of grab folks at that point in their early, early pre-careers, if you will, and teach them why this is an important subject.

So I spoke to a professor at Georgia Tech who is teaching a graduate course in LLM security and said that she was actually surprised by how much interest there's been in AI security when she teaches you know, undergraduate level sort of cyber one one and she talks about large language models, there's a lot of interest in following up outside of class and trying to learn more about that specific part of cyber.

For those of us who are perhaps a little pessimistic that college students want to focus on security when all the money and the attention is in building and deploying new products, I think this story that I wrote was kind of a somewhat of a corrective to that narrative, but also just as a source of optimism that at least according to the folks who are teaching this material, there are folks interested in learning about this kind of stuff and there are folks interested in pursuing graduate school education and getting certificates specifically in the security part of AI, which again is good to see. And I think we're going to start to see a shift over the next few years as people come out of these programs and begin entering the workforce. We're going to see a more security minded attitude, I think, toward AI development, at least if some of these colleges get their way.

DR's Rob Wright: I'm actually, I suddenly have a positive outlook, which is really rare for me. I'm normally the pessimist.

DR's Rob Wright: Thank you. Yeah, no, that's great news. it sounds like a welcome development. So maybe there is something to look forward to with AI. Fingers crossed.

CD's Eric Geller: Yeah. And the one thing I'll add is that this is not just something that's siloed at specific universities. There are coalitions of schools working together to create curriculums, curricula that that they can you know use interchangeably, taking best practices that one school has found in terms of what works for teaching in the classroom, sharing that with other schools.

This is one area where the federal government is actually kind of playing a behind the scenes role because they sponsor this nationwide coalition that has sort of different schools have taken the lead on building their own little groups of schools that they work with to kind of create lesson plans, find subject matter that works in the classroom, and then share those lessons with each other. You know, academia is obviously a very collaborative sphere, and I think that works out to everyone's benefit here because the teachers that are finding things that work are are telling other teachers and other professors in other schools, you might want to try this approach. And there's a consortium that is kind of bringing all that together and trying to make this not necessarily the exact same curriculum at every school, but shared curricula across universities.

DR's Rob Wright: That's good. I'm optimistic, and I'm never optimistic. Well, thank you guys for coming together to discuss Cybersecurity Awareness Month and I'm glad we're ending it on a positive note. Thanks guys.

TTC's Sharon Shea: Thanks, Rob. Thanks, Eric.
