#9826. Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

A security firm patched a decade-old app to prevent the takeover of millions of machines, highlighting that abandoned domains remain a boon to attackers.

When managed security service provider Eye Security spotted an odd update process in a client's telemetry that appeared to be reaching out to outdated — and in some cases, malicious — domains, the company decided to take a deeper look.

The updater belonged to a modified version of Time4Popcorn, a 2014-era BitTorrent client that allows movies to be downloaded from the Internet, and even after a decade, the persistent updater continued to run on more than 2.5 million Windows machines and an estimated 300,000 Macs, checking for new software, according to the MSSP's advisory. The problem: Many of the domains checked by the updater were open to registration, which could allow any would-be cyberattacker to register the domain and have an easy way to place software on millions of machines.

The situation highlights the issue of old infrastructure and the threat it poses to users and businesses, especially if the business's employees work from home, Niels Teusink, principal security researcher for Eye Security, wrote in the analysis.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

"[W]hile these users chose to install Popcorn Time, none of them chose to have a forgotten updater running in the background for years, ready to run any code with full privileges for whoever controlled one of its domains," the company stated in its advisory. "With millions of systems affected and the software long abandoned, there was no vendor to fix this and no patch on the way: if we didn't act, nobody would."

The risk of domains that are dropped by a legitimate service and then picked up again, or bought by a gray-market or criminal operator — sometimes called "dropcatch domains" — have become an increasing issue as developers have stopped updating, or sold off, legacy software infrastructure. In February 2025, for example, exposure management firm watchTowr discovered 150 Amazon S3 buckets that had been abandoned, so they registered and found that more than 8 million HTTP requests from government and companies came in for resources that had been hosted at those addresses.

And with AI enabling a more sophisticated analysis of software projects, attackers may be able to more quickly do the necessary research to find domains that could be a backdoor into users' systems, says Benjamin Harris, founder and CEO of watchTowr.

"AI is definitely driving the barrier-to-entry down for this kind of research very quickly," he says. "We're seeing AI used to reproduce vulnerabilities, find zero days, but applied to this, AI can be used to install a bunch of software, install network taps, see what all the software reaches out to, see what's not registered, or see what's been abandoned and what we can hijack."

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

Typically, there are two types of vulnerable domains that questionable operators might take an interest in. The first are homograph domains that look like their legitimate cousins and include both typosquatting domains, such as "gmai[.]com," that try to catch browsers whose users mistyped a URL, and lookalike domains that are used in phishing to visually fool users. The value of these types of domains to the owner varies, depending on the amount of traffic they attract, says Renée Burton, vice president of threat intelligence at cybersecurity vendor Infoblox.

However, dropcatch domains that are integrated into the supply chain for a piece of software are a completely different — and more serious — risk, she says. Infoblox has registered hundreds of domains that had been part of supply chains to prevent attackers from using them.

"Supply chain attacks can happen at a moment's notice, and depending on how dropped domains are integrated into existing software, a threat actor can quickly abuse a supply chain dropped domain to conduct sophisticated attacks that lead to data loss and ransomware," Burton says.

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

In 2024, Chinese company Funnull bought the polyfill[.]io domain from the creator of the Polyfill service and began redirecting users to tens of thousands of websites.

The Popcorn Time issue highlights the problem. Anyone with access to the domains, and with some reverse engineering, could figure out how to tinker with the legacy updaters. In fact, that's what Eye Security did, updating the code to stop the automated process of reaching out to the old domains.

"All we needed to do was supply a link to an executable and the program would download it and then execute it with high privileges (NT AUTHORITYSYSTEM)," Teusink wrote. "There was no code signing and this process was all happening over HTTP."

Eye Security stressed that another project, confusingly also named Popcorn Time, is a 2025 effort to create a legitimate streaming service and is not impacted by the legacy update issues.

Companies should know the domains that their employees are reaching out to and the reputation of those domains, and should extend that monitoring and protection to remote users, says watchTowr's Harris.

"The big challenge with things like BYOD and working from home is that now the network perimeter extends from not just your corporate network ... but the user's home network as well," he says.

The community needs to come together as well, says Infoblox's Burton. While taking active defense to the same extent as Eye Security continues to be legally problematic, finding legacy and unused infrastructure is something that security communities on the Internet can continue to work on, she says.

"Threat actors understand the value of controlling a domain which is integrated into an existing supply chain and being queried by real people on a regular basis," Burton says. "We need more defenders looking for proactive ways to disrupt domain drop schemes by purchasing high-value pending drop domains before threat actors, and by looking for ways to reduce threat actors cash out opportunities from these attacks."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

With Akismet, you also won’t have to worry about innocent comments being caught by the filter or false positives. You can simply tell Akismet about those and it will get better over time. It also checks your contact form submissions against its global spam database and weed out unnecessary fake information.

Features in Bullets:

  • The program automatically checks comments and filters out spam.
  • Hidden or misleading links are often revealed in the comment body. 
  • Akismet tracks the status of each comment, allowing you to see which ones were caught by Akismet and which ones were cleared by a moderator.
  • A spam-blocking feature that saves disk space and makes your site run faster.
  • Moderators can view a list of comments approved by each user.

Pricing

  • Free to use for personal blog 

5. Contact Form 7

Contact Form 7 is a plug-in that allows you to create contact forms that make it easy for your users to send messages to your site. The plug-in was developed by Takayuki Miyoshi and lets you create multiple contact forms on the same site; it also integrates Akismet spam filtering and lets you customize the styling and fields that you want to use in the form. The plug-in provides CAPTCHA and Ajax submitting.

Features in bullets:

  • Create and manage multiple contact forms
  • Easily customize form fields
  • Use simple markup to alter mail content
  • Add Lots of third-party extensions for additional functionality
  • Shortcode offers a way to insert content into pages or posts.
  • Akismet spam filtering, Ajax-powered submitting, and CAPTCHA are all features of this plugin.

Pricing

  • Free to use

6. Monster Insights

When you’re looking for an easy way to manage your Google Analytics-related web tracking services, Monster Insights can help. You can add, customize, and integrate Google Analytics data with ease so you’ll be able to see how every webpage performs, which online campaigns bring in the most traffic, and which content readers engage with the most. It’s same as Google Analytics

It is a powerful tool to keep track of your traffic stats. With it, you can view stats for your active sessions, conversions, and bounce rates. You’ll also be able to see your total revenue, the products you sell, and how your site is performing when it comes to referrals.

MonsterInsights offers a free plan that includes basic Google Analytics integration, data insights, and user activity metrics.

Features in bullets:

  • Demographics and interest reports:
  • Anonymize the  IPs of visitor
  • See the results of how far visitors Scroll down
  • Show the insights of multiple links to the same page and show you which links get more clicks
  • See sessions of two related sites as a single session
  • Google AdSense tracking
  • Send you weekly analytics report of your blog you can download it as pdf

Pricing

  • Premium plan= $99.50/year that comes with extra features like page and post tracking, Adsense tracking,  custom tracking and reports.

7. Pretty Links

Pretty Links is a powerful WordPress plugin that enables you to easily cloak affiliate links on your websiteIt even allows you to easily redirect visitors based on a specific request, including permanent 301 and temporary 302/307 redirects.

Pretty links also helps you to automatically shorten your url for your post and pages.

You can also enable auto-linking feature to automatically add affiliate links for certain keywords

Features

  •  Create clean, easy-to-remember URLs on your website (301, 302, and 307 redirects only)
  • Random-generator or custom URL slugs
  • Track the number of clicks
  • Easy to understand reports
  • View click details including ip address, remote host, browser, operating system, and referring site
  • You can pass custom parameters to your scripts when using pretty permalinks, and still have full tracking capability.
  • Exclude IP Addresses from Stats
  • Cookie-based system to track your activity across clicks
  • Create nofollow/noindex links
  • Toggle tracking on / off on each link.
  • Pretty Link Bookmarklet
  •  Update redirected links easily to new URLs!

Pricing

  • Beginner Plan=$79/year that can be used on 1 site
  • Marketer Plan: $99/year – that can be used on upto 2 sites
  • Super Affiliate Plan: $149/year – that can be use on upto 5 sites

#9824. Artificial Limitation: The Illusion of Intelligence

Author, technology leader, ex-competitive gamer, nerd enthusiast, father of two, husband of one, avid consumer of music.

Author, technology leader, ex-competitive gamer, nerd enthusiast, father of two, husband of one, avid consumer of music.

Author, technology leader, ex-competitive gamer, nerd enthusiast, father of two, husband of one, avid consumer of music.

Like most of the world, I increasingly leverage AI in my daily life, both in and out of work. I won’t claim to be an AI professional, but rather a professional who uses AI. In fact, I’d consider myself a professional thinker, which is perhaps what fascinates me so much about this nomenclature of Artificial Intelligence. So much so that I find myself writing another article about AI instead of focusing on my other writing initiatives.

I have repeatedly circled back to this, including in my article, AI Doesn’t Think The Way You Think It Thinks, and it comes down to what it truly means to know, to think, and to have intelligence. I don’t mean this in a philosophical sense, but in the practical sense of how we're seeing it applied today. I feel like I had a breakthrough in understanding this past week that I hope to impart in this article.

First, I want to narrow the scope of artificial intelligence to the productized service models we are generally interacting with from companies like Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and xAI. These models are how most of us are experiencing AI, and while I think a broader reflection on AI without the boundaries imposed by these companies is interesting, it's less applicable to most of us. Those boundaries are exactly where I have found the nuance lies.

In my last article, I used the term “frozen brain” to explain how these models are incapable of learning when we use them. They have already synthesized their knowledge and weighted their parameters. They might synthesize information again to satisfy a prompt, but they don't re-integrate that new synthesis into the original synthesis in the moment. Likewise, they adapt their behavior using the conversation’s context, but the context remains localized. That is inherently different from permanently learning from experience. If you’re familiar with how a computer works, it’s kind of like the difference between memory and storage. It’s in the memory; it is not in the storage.

That is because the models we use are not allowed to learn directly from these interactions, as part of safety measures to ensure stability and prevent corruption by bad actors. To be clear, your data may be used later during controlled training sessions. The difference is called in-context learning versus in-weight learning. In training mode, their weights are adjusted based on a multitude of factors related to the data used: objectives, quality, and repetition.

What’s important to understand is that AI doesn't directly retrieve files like an archive that keeps exact copies of everything it’s been trained on. In fact, it might not even know where that data came from because training doesn’t reliably preserve the connection between learned information and its original source. Instead, it uses a distributed pattern, kind of like a mind map, that spreads information across millions or billions of connections, resulting in lossiness. This is why it typically can’t recite any particular book word for word. Similar to a human, if you read a book over and over, you may be able to recall a specific passage verbatim, but if you read it only once, you may only be able to recall generalities. It’s also why it often searches the internet to validate its response, and why some people set up Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a vector database to enable that level of information retrieval for their agents.

From a repetition standpoint, LLMs memorize phrasing more than the meanings behind them. When thousands of phrases share the same pattern, the connection to that node becomes stronger. Meaning it builds its memory’s scaffolding based on familiar shape or sentence structure, not the substance. Perhaps this is one of the reasons why LLMs are prone to misinformation and hallucinations. For the record, human memory tends to be semantic.

This also means that an AI model doesn’t know why a pattern is necessarily desirable. It knows it is more prevalent than others, and it may be able to regurgitate why others say it is beneficial or harmful, but it doesn’t have its own experience to judge when, why, or whether to apply it. Perhaps this is why patterns of abstract phrases and balanced contrasts often flag AI writing detectors.

One of the most powerful drivers for human learning and behavioral change is a biological response to comfort and discomfort associated with prediction errors, the pleasure of acquisition, and loss aversion, something AI is currently unable to produce. This creates a larger question around what constitutes a learning experience. Likewise, a human may perform the same task over and over for years, but have they become better at it? If your thinking has not evolved, have you learned? There appears to be a processing of experience required to learn that is more than the acquisition of knowledge or the performance of tasks. And unlike humans, these models don't have an ongoing internal narrative. When you stop interacting with them, they aren't continuing to reflect on the conversation, reconsider their conclusions, or really think at all. The underlying model only resumes processing when prompted again.

This offers the first glimpse of AI’s inert knowledge, often conflated with activated knowledge. As disclosed in cases such as Bartz v. Anthropic and Authors Guild v. OpenAI, these models have consumed most books you could possibly think of. And yet, time and again, I am left perplexed by these models' inability to inherently apply this information, even when I have established it as a preference. Instructions say to do x, y, z, and it may perform those instructions exactly. But as the instructions grow to a, b, c, d, e, f, g, it tends to cherry-pick which instructions it consistently follows. When asked, it will acknowledge it forgot to do c and e, and it will tell you it is updating its memory so it doesn't forget those things, but it will likely do it again and again.

This made me aware of a gap in how our current models operate. AI has become very impressive with its confident, verbose responses, often outproducing a human's ability to regurgitate a line of cohesive-sounding wording, but on closer look, it appears to be just that. It actually pales in comparison to most humans’ inherent executive function. Over time, a human can create increasingly complicated actions by compounding knowledge, and we are often unaware we are even doing it. When we write, draw, cook, and so on, we are subconsciously and consciously applying lessons and preferences. Current gen AI models are limited in this way, and it’s not just my observation; there is an increasing body of research to support this: Strong Memory, Weak Control: An Empirical Study of Executive Functioning in LLM, Deficient Executive Control in Transformer Attention, Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts.

The current workaround that I and others I know have been applying to supplement this limitation is to chunk the instructions for them, similar to how humans naturally chunk information. This looks like tiered models of skills and sub-agents that roll up to an orchestrator agent. Some are even creating teams of agents where one’s job is to poke holes in the other’s outputs. This is imperfect, though, because the models themselves remain non-deterministic even with clear instructions, much like a human. However, today they likely are unable to be as consistent as a human, and they certainly don’t face the same societal pressures a human does.

Unlike traditional software, which executes rigid, rule-based code to hopefully return an identical output every time, generative AI models calculate a probability distribution for the next piece of text. The floating-point arithmetic across billions of neural network calculations involves decimal rounding that accumulates and produces different outputs. The model is then programmed to randomly pick from a pool of the most probable results, which increases the randomness of its answers. Lastly, even hardware variations can cause calculations to run at different times, producing different results. This is more prevalent when models run across massive, multi-GPU distributed clusters handling concurrent requests. All of this contributes to its non-deterministic nature.

One last thing I want to be clear about before I wrap up this explanation: while we understand AI more than ever, we still have a lot we don’t. This is something Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei exposed in his April 2025 essay; MIT Technology Review has emphasized it since early 2024, and research is still finding it to hold true as recently as August 2026. It is easy for me to confidently explain how all of this works, as an LLM chatbot might, but there is nuance here that has either been simplified for the sake of this article, simplified for my own understanding, or simply not fully understood yet. That alone should produce concern: the people making these things don’t understand how they work.

This understanding doesn’t make AI any less impressive, but it does make it apparent that it should be called Artificial Imitation. Emily Bender and her colleagues call them stochastic parrots. Now that I know this, I find myself using it differently. These models lack practical wisdom and good sense. For example, they don’t compare all of the information they have on a subject before responding. At some point, unbeknownst to me and probably even to them, they will spit out a response that may even have a source they grabbed from the internet. However, the source doesn’t always back up what it’s saying, and it may know of more conflicting sources than the one it chose. Moreover, it tends to mistake verbosity for significance. That is why I do not let it write for me, and after a trial period of having it help me polish work, I am pulling back from even that. That is also why I apply the same validation techniques to its code that I would to a human. Because at the end of the day, I am the one left accountable for what I put into the world under my name, and the jury is still out on whether or not that is intelligent.

Forget the Machine God. Fear the Machine Idiot.

Author, technology leader, ex-competitive gamer, nerd enthusiast, father of two, husband of one, avid consumer of music.

#9823. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9822. L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

I ricercatori non riescono a spiegare del tutto perché le minacce informatiche in Italia siano così diverse rispetto a quelle di qualsiasi altro Paese.

Translation provided by Dark Reading's internal AI translation tool.

Secondo nuovi dati, l’Italia è vittima di un numero sproporzionatamente elevato di attacchi informatici. Non solo: le tipologie di attacchi che colpiscono le organizzazioni nel Paese sono molto diverse da quelle che colpiscono altre località. I ricercatori avanzano tre teorie per spiegarne il motivo.

È vero che alcune regioni e alcuni paesi sono esposti a un rischio informatico maggiore a causa di fattori economici, militari e politici. Israele è una calamita per gli hacktivisti e per le minacce persistenti avanzate (APT) regionali, legate agli Stati. La storia unica del Brasile lo rende un vero e proprio alveare di trojan bancari. L’economia degli Stati Uniti attirerà sempre la massima attenzione da parte dei truffatori. Non è però così ovvio il motivo per cui l’Italia sia un bersaglio così popolare per i criminali informatici.

Related:Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

«Uno dei motivi principali per cui abbiamo deciso di esaminare il panorama delle minacce in Italia è che il Paese continuava a comparire in cima alle nostre statistiche nei rapporti interni mensili», afferma Gianluca Tiepolo, analista di criminalità informatica presso Intel471. In un rapporto condiviso in esclusiva con Dark Reading prima della sua pubblicazione, Intel471 ha rilevato che l’Italia rappresenta un vero e proprio caso a sé stante nel panorama globale delle minacce informatiche. Le organizzazioni italiane subiscono attacchi a un ritmo ben superiore a quanto ci si potrebbe ragionevolmente aspettare, considerando le dimensioni del Paese, la sua economia e la sua situazione politica. Inoltre, gli attacchi sfruttanti le vulnerabilità e le infrastrutture web sono molto più comuni in Italia che altrove.

«Volevamo capire cosa fosse alla base di quelle statistiche», afferma Tiepolo. Alla fine, però, i dati dipingono un quadro quasi inspiegabile di ciò che sta accadendo nella terra della pasta e del Chianti.

L’Italia è il 25° Paese più grande al mondo ma, secondo questi nuovi dati, le sue organizzazioni rappresentano circa il 7% di tutti i dati di accesso iniziale venduti sui forum dei criminali informatici. A livello globale, è seconda solo agli Stati Uniti (30%). L’Italia si colloca inoltre al quarto posto tra i Paesi più presi di mira dal ransomware.

Ancora più strani sono i tipi di intrusioni informatiche che colpiscono le organizzazioni in Italia. Secondo i nuovi dati, gli initial access broker (IAB) hanno ottenuto il loro primo punto d’appoggio sfruttando vulnerabilità nel 57% dei casi. Le credenziali hanno spiegato solo il 23% dei casi. Nel frattempo, gli IAB hanno venduto l’accesso all’infrastruttura web di proprietà delle vittime nel 49% dei casi, con strumenti di accesso remoto e desktop remoto che rappresentano il 26% dei casi.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

E allora? Forse queste cifre non saltano all’occhio. Ora, però, confrontiamole con i dati di Intel471 tratti dal suo rapporto “2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook”:

A livello globale nel 2025, gli IAB hanno preso di mira gli strumenti di accesso remoto e di desktop remoto nel 67% dei casi — il 41% in più, in termini relativi, rispetto all’Italia. Nel frattempo, l’infrastruttura web — di gran lunga la risorsa più a rischio in Italia — rappresentava una frazione talmente esigua dei dati globali di Intel471 che l’azienda non si è nemmeno preoccupata di citarla nel proprio rapporto.

Allo stesso modo, secondo i dati globali dell’azienda, gli attacchi basati sulle credenziali sono oggi, in generale, otto volte più comuni di qualsiasi altro tipo di attacco. È emerso che il 49% delle inserzioni su IAB indicava le credenziali come tipo di attacco, rispetto al 23% dei dati specifici per l’Italia. E, cosa davvero esilarante, mentre in Italia rappresentano circa il 57% di tutti gli attacchi, le vulnerabilità sfruttate sono emerse solo nel 6,5% dei casi a livello globale.

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Sebbene i dati sulla sicurezza informatica possano essere interpretati in modi diversi a seconda delle circostanze, l’Italia sembra davvero una sorta di “unicorno” del rischio informatico, afferma Tiepolo, aggiungendo che l’Italia è ormai da tempo in ritardo in termini di preparazione informatica.

«Sono italiano», dice. «Ho lavorato con molti clienti italiani diversi. Quello che posso dire è che l’Italia è probabilmente leggermente indietro rispetto ad altri paesi europei, semplicemente in termini di [adozione delle] tecnologie di sicurezza. Ad esempio, le tecnologie di rilevamento e risposta sugli endpoint (EDR) sono diventate popolari in Italia intorno al 2020–2021. Prima del 2020, la maggior parte delle aziende italiane non utilizzava la tecnologia EDR. Quindi, forse storicamente, l’Italia è un po’ indietro nell’investire effettivamente in prodotti e tecnologie di sicurezza informatica».

Inoltre, i criminali informatici opportunisti stanno sfruttando in massa vulnerabilità note, diffuse e spesso piuttosto datate per mietere un numero maggiore di vittime in Italia rispetto ad altri paesi. «I dati che abbiamo visto la scorsa settimana da PHP2Shell, credo, confermano questa valutazione. L’Italia è il paese europeo con il maggior numero di versioni PHP 4, 5 e 7, che sono ormai fuori supporto», osserva Tiepolo.

«Ben il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale rivolte all’Italia sono quelle che chiamiamo “offerte all’ingrosso”», ipotizza. «Non si tratta di offerte mirate specificatamente all’Italia, ma semplicemente di sfruttamento delle vulnerabilità. La nostra valutazione è che l’Italia sia probabilmente più lenta di altri paesi nell’applicare le patch ai propri sistemi».

Un’altra possibilità correlata è che l’Italia si trovi vittima di una sorta di effetto rete delle vulnerabilità informatiche. La logica è più o meno questa: se determinate tecnologie sono particolarmente diffuse in un paese come l’Italia e le organizzazioni sono lente nell’affrontare le vulnerabilità di tali tecnologie, allora quel paese diventa un’economia di scala attraente.

Come ha scritto Intel471 nel proprio rapporto: «Una volta che un attore sviluppa un metodo di sfruttamento efficace, può applicare tale metodo ad altri sistemi esposti senza dover condurre un’attività di ricognizione separata ed estesa contro ciascuna organizzazione. Ciò riduce lo sforzo necessario per compromettere aziende la cui dimensione o il cui profilo potrebbero altrimenti offrire un incentivo limitato per un’intrusione mirata».

I ricercatori non hanno potuto specificare esattamente a quali tecnologie, vulnerabilità o metodi di sfruttamento questa teoria possa riferirsi, ma hanno osservato che essa si inserisce nel dato secondo cui il 90% delle offerte di accesso iniziale alle organizzazioni italiane online viene venduto all’ingrosso.

Senza avallare specificatamente i dati o le conclusioni di Intel471, i rappresentanti della società di sicurezza informatica Cleafy, con sede a Milano, hanno dichiarato a Dark Reading di aver osservato modelli sostanzialmente simili.

«La nostra ricerca sulle minacce evidenzia effettivamente un modello correlato: gli autori degli attacchi riutilizzano strumenti, infrastrutture e tecniche per estendere le campagne a diversi obiettivi bancari italiani», ha scritto l’azienda via e-mail. Ha citato casi come il kit di iniezione web drIBAN, che gli autori degli attacchi hanno utilizzato per sfruttare il sistema di Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC), ampiamente diffuso in Italia. Casi come quello di drIBAN «non dimostrano che l’Italia abbia un mercato di accesso iniziale sproporzionatamente ampio, ma illustrano come le tecniche di attacco e le infrastrutture riutilizzabili possano aiutare i criminali informatici a estendere le operazioni su più obiettivi».

C’è un altro fattore, potenzialmente significativo, che spiega perché l’Italia appaia così diversa dagli altri paesi nei set di dati sugli attacchi informatici: la prevalenza delle piccole imprese.

La maggior parte delle imprese, ovunque, è di piccole dimensioni, ma, almeno rispetto ad altre economie avanzate, ciò è particolarmente vero in Italia. Una “panoramica dei dati per l’Italia” del maggio 2024 redatta da McKinsey ha rilevato che le “MSME” — micro, piccole e medie imprese — hanno contribuito all’economia e all’occupazione italiane in misura superiore di circa il 10% rispetto alla loro quota relativa in altre economie avanzate. Lo scorso marzo, inoltre, l’Organizzazione per la cooperazione e lo sviluppo economico (OCSE) ha pubblicato un rapporto in cui si indicava che nel 2023 il 99,9% delle imprese italiane era costituito da PMI e il 94,8% da microimprese.

«L’Italia ha molte piccole e medie imprese», afferma Tiepolo. «Una delle cose emerse dai dati — in particolare quelli relativi alle estorsioni — è che questi gruppi prendono di mira [in modo sproporzionato] le piccole e medie imprese. Quindi questo potrebbe essere uno dei motivi per cui [l’Italia si distingue] rispetto ad altri paesi che hanno un maggior numero di grandi aziende».

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9821. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

#9820. Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

A recent law enforcement operation to dismantle harmful scam centers was a big success. A threat intelligence expert walks us through what happened and why he wants more of the same.

Pushes for public-private partnerships to address escalating cyber threats have been on the industry's radar for years. Collaboration has been a focal point in cybersecurity conference panels and government initiatives. Calls for more information-sharing and analysis centers have been persistent.

As director of preemptive cyberdefense at Silent Push, Michael Sweeney had a front-row seat to this kind of partnership when his company recently took part in "Operation Blackout," a coordinated international operation to take down criminal networks operating out of West Africa.

Operation Blackout coordinated efforts by the UK's National Crime Agency, the US Department of Justice (DoJ), the FBI, and private industry partners — including Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Silent Push — to disrupt criminal networks behind pig-butchering, romance, and cryptocurrency scams. The DoJ announced that the campaign resulted in dozens of arrests, the rescue of trafficking victims, and the removal of more than 3.7 million fake social media accounts.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

As the UK's main law enforcement agency, the National Crime Agency hosted Joint Disruption Week in London in early October to bring together the DoJ and the FBI with private industry partners to share real-time intelligence. In addition to US authorities and private industry partners, the Nigerian Joint Case Team on Cybercrimes, the Nigeria Police Force-National Cybercrime Center, and Ghanaian Cyber Security Authority also participated.

The Joint Disruption Week marked the first coordinated effort specifically focused on West Africa, according to the DoJ, which noted that global commitments are essential to dismantling the far-reaching scam centers.

The goal of these operations is to tackle scam activity at the global scale it has reached today, Sweeney explains. The more people who participate, the "better off we are," he says.

"The idea is not only to stop the current scams, but also to look across all of these different events," Sweeney tells Dark Reading. "[Industry and government are] all needed together in order to get this successfully taken down."

Data taken from scams reported through the FBI's Internet Complaint Center and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre formed the initial basis for Operation Blackout. From there, law enforcement compiled information, including the domains the scammers used and the infrastructure they set up to manipulate people for money.

Then the collaboration really began. Meta provided some of the data that helped drill down to specific regions — a surprising move, since social media platforms don't generally cooperate with law enforcement, despite threat actors abusing platforms to lure in victims. Several other organizations sent signals to further paint a picture of the attacker's intent and infrastructure.

Related:AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes

Silent Push's role involved providing 35,000 domains, creating more than 70 detection rules to trigger alerts when malicious activity occurs, and fingerprinting, Sweeney says. All of those are considered the "common choke points" that help researchers and authorities map the threat actors' network patterns.

Everything was analyzed, and the data augmented each other to provide the evidence authorities needed to take down the scammers, Sweeney says.

"Once you get everyone in the room with all the data, it becomes easier to see the big picture," he says. "From that, see where the attacks are coming from, the commonalities, and who is the most important person to take down in the operation, and where you want to go to get these people."

Sweeney attributes the success of Operation Blackout and other operations he has worked on over the years to how clear the mission was; everyone was on the same page about the goals and importance of data sharing, he says. Many of the legal or jurisdiction blockers that would otherwise prevent them from sharing information and hinder actual action were removed, including data-sharing agreements with users.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

A number of providers were also involved, including Starlink. While each platform offers different services, they united in a shared stance. The camaraderie and energy that accompanied it were palpable, Sweeney says.

"We come together [to] say, 'If you're abusing our services, we're going to do everything we can to stop you, and we're going to pull in law enforcement,'" he says.

One thing Sweeney would like to change is the pace; he would like to see these partnerships move faster and conduct more operations as scammers drain billions from the US economy. Threat actors who exploit vulnerable populations and employ highly deceptive social engineering tactics are only improving faster with the help of artificial intelligence.

Sweeney says the people who just report a scam or who are too ashamed to come forward at all draw him to this work. They should know they aren't alone and that people are working hard to fight back, he adds.

"Everyone really wants to stop it, so pacing may be the only frustration," Sweeney says. "Let's do more. Hit them while they're down so that more people don't have that moment where they're having to figure out how to report a scam.”

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9818. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.
